q: A virtualised server farm is provisioned by ticket and billed annually. What can you conclude about its NIST characteristics?
a: Ticket approval prevents on-demand self-service. Check whether resources scale rapidly and whether usage is metered: annual billing alone does not prove that elasticity or measured service is absent.

q: A CFO argues: 'Providers have economies of scale, so moving our steady 24/7 batch servers to the cloud must cut our bill.' Do you agree?
a: Not as stated. Economies of scale (standardised workloads, bulk hardware, stripped-down software) lower the **provider's** unit cost, but a steady 24/7 load gains little from elasticity or paying only when needed. Compare total cost and operational needs for this workload; the case is stronger if load is spiky or the team wants to stop running hardware.

q: An internal platform lets departments create VMs from a portal in minutes and sends each department a monthly usage report, but it can only be reached from managed office desktops. Which NIST characteristic is in doubt, and which ones can't you judge yet?
a: Self-service and measured service look satisfied; **broad network access** is in doubt, because it expects access over the network through standard mechanisms from varied clients. Being internal-only is not the problem, since private clouds are valid. Resource pooling and rapid elasticity are still unknown until you know whether capacity is shared and can grow and shrink quickly.

q: A hosting firm rents fixed physical servers on 12-month contracts, reachable over the internet, and markets them as 'cloud'. Using the common thread of the cloud definitions, is the label justified?
a: No. Internet access gives only network access; the definitions share on-demand provisioning from a shared pool that is rapidly provisioned and released with minimal provider interaction. Fixed servers on long contracts are neither elastic nor on demand. The label would hold if customers could self-provision and release capacity in minutes and pay for what they use.

q: A teammate says an internal private cloud is 'not real cloud' because one industry definition describes cloud as a service delivered to many external customers. How do you respond?
a: Disagree. Gartner's wording emphasises multi-tenant delivery to external customers, but NIST, the anchor definition, is about characteristics, not who operates it. A private cloud for one organisation is cloud if it offers self-service, network access, pooled resources (shared across departments), rapid elasticity and measured service.

q: A startup expects anywhere between 1,000 and 200,000 users in its first year. Why does pay-as-you-go matter more to it than to a firm with flat, predictable load?
a: With uncertain demand, buying for peak means either a large upfront investment or running out of capacity; elasticity and usage-based spend let cost follow actual users and make experiments cheap. A firm with flat load can size owned capacity accurately, so its gain from converting CapEx to OpEx is smaller and has to be shown with a total-cost comparison.

q: A bank and a fintech startup both want to launch a new payments feature on the cloud. Why will the bank's first-year plan look different?
a: The bank carries regulatory, governance, security and privacy obligations and legacy systems that must be migrated, integrated and co-exist with the new feature, so its plan centres on migration and integration. The startup starts cloud-first on a clean slate and can spend its effort on the product. The bank's advantage is existing customers and data, which is why integration is worth the cost.

q: A team must apply a specific OS kernel patch and install custom middleware. Which service model fits, and what extra work comes with it?
a: IaaS, because it is the only model where the customer controls the OS and middleware. The cost is that the team now patches the OS, runs the middleware and configures scaling itself. If the kernel requirement went away, PaaS would remove that work, but in return you accept the provider's supported languages and runtimes.

q: An HR department needs leave management. A standard product covers 90% of its workflow, but there is one unusual approval rule. SaaS or an app built on PaaS?
a: SaaS if the rule can be expressed through the product's predefined settings, since it gives the least operational work. Build on PaaS only if the rule is essential and cannot be configured: you then write and own the application but avoid running servers. The deciding factor is whether the customisation is worth owning code for.

q: Customer data leaks from a SaaS CRM because an employee shared a report with a public link. The team blames the provider. Who is accountable?
a: The customer. Even in SaaS, where the provider operates nearly every layer, data classification, access decisions and accountability stay with the customer. The answer would differ if the leak came from a breach of the provider's own infrastructure or application, which are its layers.

q: A company runs its core system in its own data centre and its analytics on two public providers. A teammate calls this 'multi-cloud'. Is that the full description?
a: Only half. Two public providers is multi-cloud (mixing vendors), and connecting them to the on-premises private environment is hybrid (mixing cloud types). Naming both matters because hybrid raises integration and co-existence concerns between environments, while multi-cloud raises cross-vendor skills and operations concerns.

q: A team proposes a VPC to meet the rule 'customer data must not leave our premises'. Does it?
a: No. A VPC gives logical network isolation and controlled access inside the provider's infrastructure, so the data still sits on the provider's premises. The rule calls for a private cloud, or a hybrid design that keeps that data on premises. A VPC fits when the requirement is isolation with public-cloud scalability and pricing, not data location.

q: A vendor offers a pre-integrated rack of hardware and cloud software to install in your data centre. Which deployment model is this, and how does it compare with building your own private cloud?
a: A proprietary cloud: a complete hardware plus software stack, owned by the provider or sold for on-premises use. It is faster to stand up than assembling your own private cloud from parts, but you depend on that vendor's stack for upgrades and features, so you trade build effort for lock-in.

q: An exam answer for a web app's architecture says only 'use EC2, S3, RDS and CloudFront'. Why would it lose marks, and how should it be rewritten?
a: It lists product names without the need each one meets or why it was chosen. Rewrite it in capability terms (compute for the app tier, object storage for static assets, a managed relational database, a CDN at the edge) and justify each choice from the requirements. The major providers have overlapping categories, so the reasoning carries the marks, not the product name.

q: Two providers both cover compute, storage, databases, identity, ML and management tooling. Your client wants to pick one by comparing catalogue size. What should decide it instead?
a: Because the categories overlap, catalogue size says little. Decide from the workload's requirements and the cloud strategy, and finish the strategy before signing vendor contracts, which Gartner lists as a common mistake. Keep an exit strategy, and favour containers and open standards where switching cost matters.

q: A team has 3 months to leave a data centre whose lease is ending. The application has stable load and no planned changes. Cloud-hosted or cloud-native?
a: Cloud-hosted: minimal change is the only way to meet the deadline, and stable load gains little from elasticity. The team gives up the resilience, autoscaling and automation gains of a redesign, but it can make selected components cloud-optimised later, once the deadline is met.

q: The CEO announces: 'We are cloud-first. Every system moves next year, starting with our ERP.' Critique this as a strategy.
a: It makes several of Gartner's mistakes at once: an executive mandate treated as a strategy, cloud-first read as cloud-only, and starting with a critical, complex workload like ERP. A better plan involves the business, prioritises benefits, chooses suitable early workloads, and includes an exit strategy.

q: A security officer says: 'Cloud is less secure, so mission-critical systems must stay on premises.' Do you agree?
a: Not as a blanket rule: 'less secure' and 'not for mission-critical' are both listed cloud myths. Security depends on design and on the responsibility split; the provider secures its layers, and the customer must still secure its own configuration, identities and data. A specific regulatory or data-location constraint, not the myth, is the valid reason to keep a system on premises.

q: A team builds heavily on one provider's proprietary queue and database APIs to go cloud-native quickly. What risk are they taking, and how could they limit it?
a: Deep use of proprietary services raises switching cost and reduces portability. They can limit this with containers and open standards where they matter, isolate provider-specific calls behind their own interfaces, and keep an exit strategy. The trade-off is that avoiding managed proprietary services gives up some of the speed that made cloud-native attractive.

q: A retailer runs a 6-week seasonal web shop. Evening traffic is 20 times the daytime level, the team is two developers, and there is no ops staff. Recommend a service model and a deployment model, and say what would make you choose IaaS instead.
a: PaaS on a public cloud, with SaaS for commodity parts such as payments or email: the provider runs the OS and runtime, and elasticity absorbs the evening peaks without the retailer owning peak capacity. Spend follows the 6-week season instead of a year-round investment. Choose IaaS only if the shop needs OS-level control or middleware the platform doesn't support, and accept that the two developers would then patch and scale servers themselves.

q: A regulated bank must keep customer records in its own data centre but wants elastic capacity for a new customer-facing app. Recommend a deployment model, and explain why a VPC alone is not enough.
a: Hybrid cloud: keep customer records in the on-premises private environment and run the elastic front end on public cloud, connected through controlled integration. A VPC gives logical isolation inside the provider's infrastructure but does not keep data on the bank's premises. The costs are governance, integration and co-existence work across two environments, plus the latency of calls back to on-premises data.

q: An enterprise wants its first cloud project to be moving its 15-year-old, heavily customised ERP. Advise on whether it should go first, and compare IaaS, PaaS and SaaS for it when it does move.
a: Advise against making it first: Gartner warns against starting with critical, complex, large workloads like ERP, so build skills on simpler workloads first. When it moves, IaaS (cloud-hosted lift and shift) keeps the customisation and needs the least change but keeps all the OS and middleware work. PaaS needs re-platforming. SaaS removes most of the operations but forces the business onto predefined settings, which may mean dropping years of customisation.

q: A proposal says: 'Move to the cloud to save money, and use two providers so disaster recovery is automatic.' Evaluate both claims and say what evidence you would want.
a: Both are listed myths or mistakes: cloud is not always cheaper, and multi-cloud does not by itself save money or improve DR; it adds cross-provider skills and operations. Ask for a workload-by-workload cost comparison, a prioritised list of benefits, and a tested DR design with recovery targets. Multi-cloud may still be justified for specific reasons, but it should come with an exit strategy rather than an assumed benefit.

q: An IT department rebrands its virtualisation cluster as 'our private cloud'. Developers can create VMs from a portal in minutes, but capacity is fixed at 200 VMs, adding hosts takes a 6-week purchase, and there is no usage reporting. Assess the claim against NIST and recommend what would close the gaps.
a: Partly justified: the portal gives on-demand self-service, and a shared cluster suggests resource pooling. It fails rapid elasticity, because the 200-VM cap and 6-week purchase stop capacity from growing quickly, and it fails measured service, because nothing is metered. Virtualisation alone is not a private cloud. To close the gaps, add per-team usage metering and either keep spare capacity or burst to public cloud (a hybrid model) so capacity can grow on demand.

q: A company is about to move 40 applications to the cloud and asks whether its existing solution architects can simply take this on. What gap would a cloud architect fill?
a: A solution architect designs a solution for a given set of requirements; the cloud architect owns the cloud strategy across them: migration plans for existing apps, the design of new cloud-native apps, oversight of cloud management and governance policies. Without that role, 40 separate solution designs would each make their own cloud choices. A small estate could combine the roles, but the strategy and governance work still has to be owned by someone.

q: Users complain that a reporting portal's data is correct but hard to find and interpret, while the DBA says the schema is well normalised. Which architect role should look at this, and why not the other?
a: The information architect, who focuses on how users experience and interact with data. The data architect designs and manages data structures, and the schema is already sound, so the problem is presentation and navigation rather than storage.

q: An enterprise with 200 on-premises VMs and a board deadline wants to start its cloud adoption with lift and shift to IaaS. Is that a sound first step, and what should it not assume?
a: Yes, as a first step: it changes little and moves infrastructure spend to a usage-based operating model quickly. It should not assume lower or predictable total spend, because predictable unit prices still depend on sizing and usage, and a lifted app gains little elasticity. Plan which applications to redesign later.

q: Two new projects arrive: an IoT telemetry service with unpredictable device growth, and an internal timesheet tool used by 50 staff. Which should be cloud-native and which can simply be cloud-enabled?
a: The IoT service should be cloud-native: greenfield, heavily dependent on elasticity and needing automatic scaling under load or failure. The timesheet tool has small, steady load, so moving it as is (cloud-enabled) is enough. Native design is only worth its cost where elasticity, statelessness and automation actually pay off.

q: A teammate says 'it isn't cloud-native unless it runs on Kubernetes with microservices.' Do you agree?
a: No. Orchestrated containers and microservices are common ways to build cloud-native apps, but the defining idea is design for cloud properties such as elasticity, automation and easy integration. A serverless app or a well-designed monolith that scales and recovers automatically can also qualify.

q: A team has containers running under a container runtime on three VMs and says they are ready for production. What is missing?
a: A runtime only executes containers. Production also needs orchestration for deployment, scaling and failure recovery, networking, CI/CD, observability, configuration management, security controls and an API gateway for external traffic. Add persistent storage and messaging if the services need them. Without orchestration, a crashed container or failed VM needs manual recovery.

q: A platform has 6 services behind an API gateway. The team wants a service mesh as well. Would you add it now?
a: Probably not yet. The gateway already handles external north-south traffic; a mesh manages internal east-west traffic (load balancing, encryption, retries), which pays off when many services need uniform inter-service policy. With 6 services, library-level retries and TLS may be enough. Revisit when the service count or the need for mutual TLS and traffic policy grows.

q: Orders must reach billing, shipping and analytics, and billing is sometimes down for maintenance. Synchronous HTTP API calls or event streaming and messaging?
a: Event streaming or messaging: the order service publishes once, each consumer processes at its own pace, and billing catches up after maintenance instead of failing the order. The cost is eventual consistency and an extra platform to operate. Keep a synchronous API where the caller needs an immediate answer, such as a price check.

q: A legacy app costs a lot to run on lifted VMs because it can't scale down at night. Would you do a complete refactor, a partial refactor or stay lifted?
a: A partial refactor is the usual first answer: target the component that blocks scale-down, such as extracting the stateless web tier so it can autoscale. A complete refactor is justified only if measured long-term gains outweigh its higher cost, time and risk. Staying lifted is fine if the night-time waste is smaller than the refactoring cost.

q: After a regional outage, the team rebuilds its whole network and cluster from IaC in another region in 20 minutes, but the app still won't start. What was most likely missing from the DR plan?
a: IaC recreates infrastructure, not state. The data, secrets and configuration the app needs were probably not restored or replicated to the recovery region. The DR plan needs data backups or replication and a way to restore secrets and config alongside the IaC, and it needs to be tested end to end.

q: Engineers fix production servers by hand during incidents, and test now behaves differently from production. How does IaC address this, and what discipline does it require?
a: Defining environments in versioned, reviewed code with deliberate parameter differences gives consistent dev, test and prod and removes untracked manual changes. The discipline is that every change, including incident fixes, goes through the code and the pipeline. Otherwise drift returns, and the next apply may overwrite the hand fix.

q: A scan finds a shell and package manager in a production image that runs as root and is patched in place. Which image practices does this break, and what would you change?
a: It breaks minimal or distroless base, non-root execution and immutable releases. Rebuild from a verified minimal or distroless base, run as a non-root user, sign the image, and replace containers with a new patched image instead of patching them in place. This shrinks the attack surface and limits what an attacker can do after a compromise. The cost is harder interactive debugging.

q: A firm containerised every app and runs them on Kubernetes in two clouds, and now says it can 'move any workload between clouds in an hour'. What has it overlooked?
a: Containers and Kubernetes definitions standardise packaging and orchestration (multi-cloud 2.0), but data, IAM policies, networking and dependencies on proprietary managed services do not move with the image. A workload using one provider's managed database still needs its data migrated and its integration rewritten. The claim holds only for stateless apps with portable dependencies.

q: A company uses a broker to place its HR system on one cloud and its analytics on another, and each app stays in its own cloud. Which multi-cloud generation is this, and what does it fail to give?
a: Multi-cloud 1.0: workloads are spread across clouds, but each app is tied to one provider. It does not give workload portability; moving an app means migrating it. Multi-cloud 2.0 containerises workloads so they can be recreated elsewhere, at the cost of running Kubernetes consistently in each cloud.

q: You must design a cloud platform for a new government agency. Should you start from a vendor's reference architecture or a neutral one such as NIST 500-292?
a: Use a neutral one to frame the actors and building blocks, then a vendor's reference architecture once the provider is chosen. NIST 500-292 or CCRA keeps the design vendor-neutral and helps the agency compare options. Vendor reference architectures are concrete starting points with proven component combinations, but they lean toward that vendor's services.

q: An online game's player count jumps 10 times during weekend events, and a zone outage last month took it offline. What two design features address these problems, and what does each cost?
a: Auto-scaled web and app tiers absorb the event spikes, and spreading them across two Availability Zones behind a load balancer keeps the game up if one zone fails. Autoscaling needs stateless servers, with sessions moved to an in-memory cache. Two zones add cross-zone replication and traffic cost.

q: The DR design uses a synchronous standby in a second AZ and snapshots copied to another region. A manager asks why both are needed. Explain, including what each one loses.
a: The synchronous standby covers zone failure with almost no data loss and fast failover, but it does nothing if the whole region fails. Cross-region snapshots cover a regional disaster, but they recover only to the last copied snapshot and need time to restore a new instance. Choose snapshot frequency against acceptable data loss and restore capacity against acceptable downtime.

q: An e-commerce team must choose between a classic stack (load-balanced, auto-scaled app servers with a shared relational database) and a serverless design with Product, Payment, Inventory and Cart functions behind an API gateway, each with its own store. Traffic is low most of the year with sharp sale peaks. Which fits, and what do you give up?
a: Serverless fits: functions scale with the sale peaks and cost little in quiet months, and separate stores let each service scale and change independently. You give up simple cross-service transactions and joins, since inventory and payment consistency now needs coordination, and you accept function limits and cold starts. A steady, high base load would favour the classic stack.

q: A company runs a 10-year-old monolith on premises. The data-centre contract ends in 6 months, and the checkout module struggles at month-end peaks. Recommend a migration approach, and say what would justify a complete refactor.
a: Lift and shift to IaaS first to meet the 6-month deadline with minimal change, then partially refactor the checkout module, for example by extracting it as a stateless, autoscaled service. Leave the rest of the monolith alone until measured benefits justify more work. A complete refactor is justified only if long-term performance and operating-cost gains outweigh its higher cost, time and risk. Note that the lifted monolith may cost more to run than expected until it is optimised.

q: A platform team manages dev, test and prod by hand, and an outage last quarter took 3 days to recover. Justify Infrastructure as Code, explain how you would keep the environments consistent but deliberately different, and say what IaC will not solve.
a: Use shared, versioned IaC modules with explicit per-environment parameters (sizes, replica counts) and separate state. Changes go through Git review and are applied automatically, which reduces drift and documents the environment. A rebuild then takes minutes instead of days. IaC will not restore data, secrets or application configuration, so DR also needs backups or replication and a tested recovery runbook.

q: A regulated insurer must keep policyholder data on premises, wants elastic capacity for quote calculations, and its CTO also wants a second public cloud 'to avoid lock-in'. Design the strategy and judge the second cloud.
a: Hybrid: keep policyholder data in the private environment and run stateless quote calculation on public cloud, sending only the data it needs over a secured link. Add a second public cloud only for a concrete reason, such as a lock-in risk or a best-of-breed service. Containerising workloads on Kubernetes makes them portable (multi-cloud 2.0), but data, identity and managed-service dependencies still tie them to a provider. Every added environment increases integration, skills and management cost.

q: A startup runs 12 containerised microservices and has had two outages: one from a bad manual deployment and one from a retry storm between services. What components would you add to make the platform production-ready, and which outage does each address?
a: Add CI/CD with automated tests and rollback to address the bad manual deployment, plus orchestration that does rolling updates and health-checks containers. For the retry storm, add observability to see call chains, and either a service mesh or consistent client libraries for retry limits, timeouts and circuit breaking. At 12 services a mesh is defensible but adds operating cost. Also add an API gateway, secure images and config management, and test resilience with failure injection.

q: Design the architecture for an online game with spiky weekend traffic, global players downloading large assets, real-time leaderboards, and a target of surviving a full region outage. Explain each component's purpose.
a: Auto-scaled web and app tiers across two AZs behind a load balancer handle the spikes and zone failure. An in-memory cache holds sessions and leaderboards so servers stay stateless and reads are fast. Object storage and a CDN serve large assets close to players. A replicated database with a synchronous standby covers zone failure. For a region outage, copy snapshots to a second region and restore them with automation, accepting data loss back to the last snapshot and a restore delay.

q: A change that passed in test fails in production, and the team finds production was hand-edited months ago. How would IaC have prevented this, and does it mean test must be identical to production?
a: If the same reviewed modules build every environment and all changes go through code, the hand edit could not have drifted unnoticed, and version history would show what changed. It does not require identical environments: size, access and region should be explicit parameters. Drift only stays away if nobody makes manual changes outside the code.

q: VMs and databases are created correctly from templates, but an app fails because a library version on the VMs differs from the one expected. Which IaC component is missing, and which would not help?
a: Configuration management, which makes sure the software on provisioned resources is set up as intended. Provisioning only created the resources correctly, and orchestration manages deployment workflows and scaling, so neither addresses what is installed on the VMs. Baking the dependency into an immutable image is another way to solve it.

q: Three product teams each copy and edit the same 800-line network template, and a security fix had to be made in three places. Which IaC best practices would you apply?
a: Modular design: extract a reusable, versioned networking module that every team consumes with its own parameters, so a fix is made once and rolled out. Add environment segmentation so Dev, Test and Prod are isolated, and state management so each apply knows the current infrastructure. The trade-off is that changes to a shared module need versioning and testing, because one change now affects every team.

q: Two engineers run applies against the same environment at the same time and resources end up duplicated. Which best practice was missing, and why does it matter?
a: State management: the tooling needs one tracked record of the current infrastructure, kept in one shared place that every apply reads and updates. Without it, each apply works from a different view of reality, and updates or scaling create duplicates or destroy resources unexpectedly.

q: In one project, the function, API and table are defined in the IaC template, but permissions and logging are configured by hand in the console afterwards. What is the risk?
a: The security and observability settings are not versioned, so a redeploy or a new environment can come up without them, or with different permissions. The lecture's serverless template defines permissions and logging alongside the resources so they deploy the same way every time. The cost is a larger template that must be reviewed carefully.

q: A containerised app reaches its database over a public endpoint protected by IP firewall rules. A reviewer asks for private endpoints in the virtual network and a role assignment for the cluster instead. What does each change gain, and what does it cost?
a: A private endpoint keeps database traffic on the private network, so the database is not exposed to the internet at all; firewall rules on a public endpoint can be misconfigured or bypassed by a compromised allowed address. A role assignment grants the cluster identity-based access, so no secret has to be stored and rotated. The costs are more network design and harder access for tools outside the network.

q: A company is all-in on one cloud and is choosing between that provider's native declarative IaC and Terraform. What should decide it?
a: If everything lives on one provider, native tools are designed for its services and model them directly, which favours them. Terraform is the better choice if the company expects to span clouds or wants one language and workflow across providers. The trade-off is depth on one cloud versus portability of skills and tooling.

q: One Terraform configuration creates clusters on three providers. A manager says 'we now have one cross-cloud cluster'. Is that right?
a: No. It provisions separate clusters with a common tool and workflow. Connectivity between them, federated identity, workload placement, scaling and logging still have to be designed and configured, and GitOps can keep workload definitions in sync. A common tool reduces the provisioning work but does not make the clusters one system.

q: An operator scales a Deployment by hand with a command during an incident. Ten minutes later it is back to its old size. Why, and what should they have done?
a: Under GitOps the declared state in Git is the source of truth, and the sync tool reconciled the live cluster back to it. The change should be made as a reviewed Git commit, or reconciliation paused deliberately during the incident with the fix committed afterwards. This is the declarative model working as intended: imperative changes do not last.

q: A bad release is reverted in Git and the cluster syncs, but the app still fails. What does a Git rollback not undo?
a: Reverting a commit restores the desired configuration, but not persistent data or a database schema migration the new version already applied. If the old version can't read the new schema, the rollback fails. Plan backward-compatible schema changes or a data recovery step, and check that the cluster has actually converged before declaring recovery.

q: In an event-driven pipeline, every component is provisioned with a single broad service identity because it was quicker. What would you change in the IaC, and why there?
a: Give each component its own identity with only the permissions it needs, for example publish-only for the producer and write-only to the analytics table for the processor. Defining this in IaC applies the least-privilege policy the same way every time and keeps it under review. The cost is more identities and policies to manage, but a compromised component can no longer reach everything.

q: A company's Dev, Test and Prod environments keep drifting apart, two engineers sometimes apply changes at the same time, and 30% of production deployments fail. Propose an IaC-based remedy and say what discipline it requires from the team.
a: Define all infrastructure in reusable, versioned modules in Git, with each environment as a separate, isolated set of parameters (environment segmentation). Keep one shared, tracked state so concurrent applies work from the same view, and apply only through a pipeline after review. Configuration management or immutable images keep the software consistent too. It only works if nobody changes infrastructure by hand; incident fixes must also go through code.

q: Choose IaC tooling for (a) a 5-person startup building only on one provider's serverless services and (b) an enterprise running Kubernetes on three providers. Justify each, and say what each choice gives up.
a: (a) The provider's native declarative IaC: it is designed for that cloud's services and can define functions, APIs, tables, permissions and logging in one template. It gives up portability if the startup later spans clouds. (b) Terraform with a provider per cloud and reusable cluster modules, plus GitOps for the workloads: one language and workflow across clouds. It gives up some native depth, and connectivity and federated identity still have to be designed separately.

q: Design the IaC for an event-driven pipeline: messages are ingested, processed by functions and written to an analytics store. A security review requires that a compromised processor cannot read or delete other data. Explain the security decisions in the template.
a: Provision the topic, subscription, function and analytics tables in one declarative configuration, with monitoring and logging defined alongside. Give each component its own identity: the processor can only consume from its subscription and write to its table. Because the IaC defines these permissions, they are reviewed and applied the same way in every environment. The trade-off is more identities to manage, in exchange for a much smaller blast radius.

q: A team uses GitOps for its Kubernetes platform. A release that adds a database column fails, and an engineer proposes 'just revert the commit'. Explain what GitOps gives here and what the revert will and will not fix.
a: GitOps keeps the declared state in Git and lets automation reconcile the cluster to it, which gives traceability, review and a quick way back to the previous configuration. Reverting restores the old Deployment, but the schema change has already been applied. If the old version can't work with the new column, the app still fails. Use backward-compatible migrations or a data recovery step, and verify convergence before calling it fixed.

q: A reviewer compares two IaC designs for a containerised app and its database. Design A exposes the database on a public endpoint with IP allow-lists and stores a database password in the cluster. Design B places the database behind a private endpoint in the virtual network, puts a web application firewall at the edge, and grants the cluster a role assignment. Which would you approve, and what does B cost?
a: Approve B. The private endpoint removes public exposure of the database, the WAF filters malicious traffic at the edge, and identity-based role assignment removes a long-lived secret that could leak. Defining all of this in the template means the same controls are present in every environment. B costs more network design, and tools outside the network can't reach the database without a controlled path.

q: A team moved from VMs to containers to cut scale-out time, but new replicas still take 90 seconds to serve traffic. What is the likely cause, and what would you check?
a: Containers skip booting a guest OS because they share the host kernel, but pulling a large image, loading dependencies and initialising the application can still dominate startup. Check the image size and pull time, and how long the application takes to warm up. Smaller images and lighter initialisation help more than changing the isolation boundary.

q: A legacy app needs a Windows kernel feature, and a second workload from a different tenant must run on the same hosts with strong separation. VMs or containers for each?
a: VMs for both. The legacy app needs its own OS, which a container sharing the host kernel cannot provide, and a hypervisor boundary gives stronger separation between tenants than process-level isolation. You give up the lighter weight and faster startup of containers, which matter less for these two requirements.

q: A company with a 3-person IT team wants to migrate to the cloud this year but has no cloud skills. Should it run the migration itself or use a managed cloud service, and what is the catch?
a: A managed cloud service fits: a provider takes on migration, configuration, optimisation, security and maintenance, usually on subscription, so the small team gets cloud benefits without building every skill first. The catch is the ongoing subscription cost and dependence on the provider. The contract must be in place before migrating, and the company still owns its data and decisions.

q: A university wants a private IaaS cloud on its own hardware and asks what a hypervisor alone would be missing. Using OpenStack's components, explain.
a: A hypervisor runs VMs, but an IaaS cloud also needs networking, block and object storage, identity, VM images, a self-service dashboard and orchestration. OpenStack supplies these (for example Neutron, Cinder, Swift, Keystone, Glance, Horizon, Heat) on top of compute (Nova). Without them, users still depend on administrators to wire each VM together, which fails on-demand self-service.

q: A security team won't allow extra agents on production servers but wants the servers' configuration managed as code. Does Ansible fit, and what does it still need?
a: Yes: Ansible is agentless, so no resident agent has to be installed on each target. It still needs a reachable management connection, credentials, and whatever prerequisites its modules require on the target. The security team's concern then shifts to protecting those credentials and the control node.

q: An engineer calls an Ansible playbook a Heat template 'because both are YAML' and wants to feed the playbook to Heat. What is wrong?
a: YAML is only the file syntax. Ansible runs a playbook's ordered tasks; Heat interprets HOT templates to orchestrate OpenStack resources. Each tool needs its own format. Either can describe infrastructure as code, so choose by whether you need OpenStack-native orchestration or general provisioning and configuration across systems.

q: A team's API uses a managed database, a queue and CI/CD, and needs no OS changes. A second system is a backup server that needs custom storage drivers. Which fits PaaS and which IaaS?
a: The API fits PaaS: it consumes managed platform services, and the platform takes over deployment, scaling and runtime management. The backup server needs server-level control of drivers and storage, so it fits IaaS. With PaaS the team still configures access and secures its own code.

q: A vendor pitch says moving to PaaS will 'cut delivery time from months to hours'. How would you treat this claim in a business case?
a: As an illustrative benefit, not a guaranteed saving. PaaS removes server setup and platform operations, which can shorten delivery a great deal, but the real gain depends on how much of the current delay is infrastructure work rather than design, testing or approvals. Measure the current lead time and its causes before promising a figure.

q: A multi-tenant SaaS platform plans to run every customer's code in containers on shared hosts. A security reviewer objects. What is the concern, and what are the options?
a: Containers isolate processes through kernel namespaces and cgroups but share the host kernel, so a kernel exploit can reach other tenants. VMs isolate at the hardware level through a hypervisor and come with established security tooling. The options are VM-per-tenant (stronger isolation, more overhead), or containers grouped onto VMs by tenant, which keeps most of the containers' speed.

q: A firm must leave its data centre in 4 months and its apps are over-provisioned. Lift-and-shift or lift-and-optimise?
a: Lift-and-shift for most apps, because the deadline and low initial change matter most. It will carry the over-provisioning into the cloud, so budget for right-sizing and optimisation after cutover. Lift-and-optimise would lower ongoing TCO and improve ROI sooner, but it takes longer and costs more up front, which the 4-month window doesn't allow.

q: A business owner says 'our app is too expensive, let's rewrite it as microservices'. Using the six drivers, what would you check before agreeing?
a: Diagnose first. If the driver is cost (infrastructure too expensive for the value), Rehost or Replatform may fix it far more cheaply. A rewrite is justified when the drivers are business fit, innovation or agility, meaning the app can't meet needs or change fast enough. A cause-effect analysis shows whether the problem is functional, architectural or technological, and the option should fix that cause.

q: The migration roadmap lists 'do not move' and 'decommission' as paths alongside lift-and-shift and refactor. Why is it worth assessing every application before picking a default path?
a: Migration is a decision per application. Some apps are better left in place or switched off, and moving them wastes effort and adds cloud cost. Discovering and assessing each app first, then planning and sequencing by dependency, avoids migrating something only to retire it later. The cost is the time spent on discovery before anything moves.

q: A bank wants its transaction system on a managed cloud database but cannot touch the business logic. Rehost or Replatform?
a: Replatform: it swaps the platform (the database) with minimal compatibility changes while code structure and features stay the same. Rehost would move the app with its existing self-managed database unchanged. Replatform adds testing for database compatibility in exchange for less database operations work.

q: After a Rehost, the business asks why the app's features and slow reports didn't improve. Is the migration a failure?
a: No, if the goal was infrastructure. Rehost changes only where the app runs, so its benefits are infrastructure ones: scaling at peaks, less hardware upkeep, redundancy, remote access and the provider's security posture. Faster reports or new features need Replatform (for example a managed analytics service) or deeper options. Set those expectations in the business case.

q: A retailer's app runs fine but the database can't cope with holiday peaks, and the code must not change. What option fits, and what would push you further along the spectrum?
a: Replatform onto a managed database and auto-scaling, which addresses the peaks without touching code structure. If the code itself blocks scaling, for example through shared state in the app tier, Replatform won't be enough and Rearchitect becomes the option, at higher cost and risk.

q: An app's features are fine, but one module can't scale and every change is risky because of technical debt. A teammate proposes Rebuild. Do you agree?
a: Rearchitect is the better fit. It restructures the existing code without changing external behaviour, for example by extracting the bottleneck module so it scales independently, and it reduces technical debt. Rebuild rewrites everything and carries the highest cost and risk, which is justified only when new capabilities such as mobile-first, IoT or AI are needed.

q: A mainframe holds valuable pricing logic that a new mobile app needs, but the mainframe is too risky to change this year. Retain, Encapsulate or Rebuild?
a: Encapsulate: expose the pricing data and functions as APIs so the mobile app can use them without rewriting the internals. Plain Retain would leave the logic inaccessible to the new app, and Rebuild is the risk the business wants to avoid. The cost is that the legacy system stays in place, and its performance and availability now limit the new app.

q: A department's expense tool is home-grown, offers nothing unique, and its developer has left. Which option fits, and what goes with it?
a: Replace with a COTS or SaaS product, taking current requirements into account, and Retire the old tool as part of the move. It is not a differentiator, so owning code adds no value. The cost is that users adapt to the product's workflow, and data has to be migrated before decommissioning.

q: Rebuild scores highest on value in Gartner's comparison. Why is it not the default answer?
a: It also has the highest cost of change, the highest risk and a long time to value. If the diagnosed drivers only call for infrastructure or platform fixes, Rehost or Replatform give faster, cheaper, lower-risk results. Choose the lightest option that fixes the drivers, and keep Rebuild for when business logic or UX must change.

q: Leadership wants the first cloud migration to be the system with the biggest projected ROI, a customer-facing billing platform. How do you respond?
a: Push back. The seven-step plan says to start simple and prioritise learning over ROI: the first project should be low-risk and highly instructive, because early success builds skills and buy-in. A billing platform is strategically important and high-risk, so a failure would set back the whole programme. Migrate it in a later wave, once the landing zone and operating model have been proven.

q: Two candidate first workloads score the same on architecture, security, availability and performance. One team is eager, the other was told to migrate. Which would you pick?
a: The eager team's workload. Team enthusiasm is one of the eight classification criteria because migrations need the owning team's engagement, and a willing team makes an early success and useful lessons more likely. The other workload can follow once there is a proven pattern to copy.

q: Six months into migration, a CFO sees costs higher than before and wants to stop. What is the likely explanation, and what would you show?
a: The migration bubble: duplicate environments, training, consultants, tools and lease penalties raise costs temporarily before old infrastructure is retired and optimisation starts. Show lifetime TCO against the baseline and the dates when on-premises costs stop. If the business case never showed savings, or retirement keeps slipping, the CFO's concern is valid.

q: An app processes citizens' health records and must stay within national borders. The preferred provider has no local region. How does this assessment concern affect the plan?
a: Jurisdiction and regulation can rule out regions or providers, so that provider is excluded for this app no matter what else it offers. Options include another provider with a local region, a private or hybrid placement for the records, or keeping the app on premises (Retain). Encryption and privacy controls are still needed, but they don't remove a data-location rule.

q: A portfolio analysis assigns Rehost to an app with 2 years of remaining life and high audit risk. Which assessment concerns would make you question that choice?
a: Architecture (life expectancy) and risk (audit, contractual). With 2 years left, Retain or Retire may cost less than migrating, and audit risk means checking compliance in the target environment before moving. The planning framework expects each app's R to come from these concerns, not from a default.

q: A company's CRM is not a differentiator, has simple processes, and needs specialist skills it cannot hire. What sourcing and hosting model would you suggest?
a: All three sourcing factors point to a partner, and the hosting would most likely be SaaS. That makes it effectively a Replace decision. The company gives up deep customisation and control of the roadmap, which is acceptable for a non-differentiating capability.

q: A trading firm's pricing engine is its main differentiator and has complex logic, but it needs rare low-latency skills. The sourcing factors conflict. How do you decide?
a: Differentiation carries the most weight (60% in the example), so the engine stays internally sourced even though skills point to a partner. Address the skills gap by hiring or training, or use a partner only for specialised infrastructure work. Validate the decision with stakeholders, because the weights are a decision aid, not a rule.

q: Using the example weights, a capability scores differentiation 3, complexity 2 and skills 1. What does the result suggest, and what should you do with it?
a: 3 × 0.6 + 2 × 0.2 + 1 × 0.2 = 2.4, which leans toward internal sourcing in the example. Skills is scored inversely, so the 1 means highly specialised skills are needed, which is a real gap to plan for. Validate against actual skills and constraints, and test risky choices with a proof of concept.

q: A hospital's 15-year-old on-premises patient scheduling system slows down at morning peaks. The code is stable and meets business needs, but the database server is end-of-life, and patient data must stay in the country. Recommend a migration option, justify it with the drivers, and name two risks to manage.
a: The drivers are risk (end-of-life platform) and scalability, not business fit, so Replatform: move to a managed database and auto-scaling in an in-country region, with minimal code change. Rebuild would add cost and risk without fixing anything the business needs. Manage database compatibility (test on the new engine, ideally with a proof of concept) and compliance (jurisdiction, privacy, encryption). Budget for the migration bubble while both environments run.

q: A firm must exit its data centre in 6 months, with 80 apps, many over-provisioned. The CFO expects savings in year one. Compare lift-and-shift and lift-and-optimise, recommend a mix, and respond to the CFO.
a: Lift-and-shift needs the least initial change and fits the deadline, but it carries over-provisioning and inefficiency. Lift-and-optimise lowers ongoing TCO but takes longer and costs more up front. Recommend lift-and-shift for most apps, sequenced by dependency and risk, with optimisation only for a few high-cost apps that can be done in time, and right-sizing after cutover. Tell the CFO that year one includes the migration bubble (duplicate environments, training, lease penalties), so savings depend on retirement and optimisation afterwards.

q: Design a portfolio assessment for an organisation with 200 applications and a 2-year programme. How would you decide each app's R, and which app would you migrate first?
a: Establish a baseline: the drivers, an inventory and dependency map, and the application concerns (performance, architecture, financial, risk, operations, security and compliance). Diagnose each app's problem with the six drivers, then assign the lightest R that fixes it, using the sourcing and hosting scoring to decide who runs it and where. Choose the first migration on the eight criteria: low-risk, instructive, with an enthusiastic team, not the highest ROI. Then iterate in waves and compare TCO against the baseline.

q: An insurer's 30-year-old policy system holds valuable rules, is nearly impossible to change, and is due to be replaced by a SaaS product in 3 years. A new mobile app needs policy data now. Choose between Retain, Encapsulate and Rebuild, and say what changes if the SaaS project is cancelled.
a: Encapsulate: expose policy data and functions through APIs so the mobile app can use them now, hiding the internals, while the system stays in place until the planned Replace. Rebuild would duplicate work the SaaS replacement will make redundant, and plain Retain would leave the mobile app without data. The legacy system's availability and performance now limit the mobile app. If the SaaS project is cancelled, revisit the drivers: a Rearchitect or Rebuild behind the same APIs becomes the long-term path, and the APIs let you swap the implementation without breaking the app.

q: A team migrating a 3-tier app proposes containers instead of VMs for the web and app tiers, keeping the database on a VM. Evaluate the proposal, including where containers would be the wrong choice.
a: Reasonable for stateless web and app tiers: containers are lighter, usually start faster, package the app consistently, and let each tier scale on its own. Keep the database on a VM or move it to a managed database if it needs OS-level tuning or strong isolation. Containers would be the wrong choice where a workload needs a different OS kernel or strong tenant separation, because they share the host kernel. Actual startup gains depend on image size and application initialisation.

q: A team hands in an architecture made of polished diagrams only. Infrastructure is still set up by hand from a wiki page. Using the instructor's framing, what is missing?
a: Architecture has two audiences: people, through diagrams and views, and machines, through IaC, YAML and properties files. In cloud native work, the provisioning code is part of the architecture, so without it the design can't be reproduced or checked against what is running. Add versioned IaC and config alongside the diagrams.

q: A messaging app and a video-streaming service are both being designed by the same team, and a manager wants one standard architecture and stack for both. Is that sensible?
a: Probably not. Different problem types lead to different architectures and stacks: messaging needs many long-lived connections and low-latency delivery, while streaming needs large content delivery and catalogue and recommendation workloads. Share platform tooling where it helps, but let each domain's constraints drive its design decisions.

q: To hit an MVP date, a team skips automated tests and hardcodes config, and records none of it. Six months later, every change breaks something. What went wrong, and what should they have done?
a: The shortcuts became hidden technical debt, which the instructor calls the 'secret list': future costs that stakeholders can't see or prioritise. Shortcuts can be a valid trade-off for an MVP, but each one should be recorded in the backlog with its consequence and a remediation item, next to the functional and non-functional requirements.

q: An on-premises three-tier app is moved one-to-one to cloud equivalents (managed DNS, CDN, load balancer, VMs or containers, managed database). What does this gain, and what doesn't it change?
a: It gains managed components, possibly with autoscaling and automatic replacement of failed instances, while keeping the broad tier structure. It doesn't create independently deployable business services, so release coordination and whole-app scaling stay the same. Redesign further only where a specific delivery or scaling problem justifies it.

q: The on-premises database pair must survive a server failure. Active-active or active-passive?
a: Active-passive if the goal is simple failover: a standby takes over when the primary fails, with straightforward consistency, but the standby's capacity is idle. Active-active if both nodes must serve load: better use of capacity and no failover delay, but concurrent writes need conflict handling or partitioning. Choose by write pattern and acceptable complexity.

q: In the cloud-native version, internal calls go through a service mesh using gRPC, and external traffic comes through an API gateway. Why split it this way rather than routing everything through the gateway?
a: The gateway handles north-south concerns at the edge: firewalling, throttling, identity and monitoring for public endpoints. The mesh handles east-west service-to-service traffic with consistent routing, encryption and telemetry, and gRPC is efficient for internal calls. Sending internal traffic through the gateway would add a hop and make it a bottleneck and single point of failure.

q: A component generates invoices once a night for 10 minutes, and another serves a 24/7 API. Function, container or VM for each?
a: The nightly job could be a function if it fits within execution limits, or a scheduled container job if it needs more time or runtime control, since containers can also run short jobs. The 24/7 API fits containers, or VMs if it needs OS-level control, because always-on load removes the pay-per-invocation advantage. Check startup, state and cost rather than assuming the packaging decides them.

q: A team runs 60 containers by hand on 8 machines with Docker. Failed containers stay down until someone notices. What does this show about why Kubernetes emerged?
a: Docker made it easy to build and run single containers, but running many across many machines needs scheduling, scaling and self-healing. Kubernetes, drawing on Google's Borg and Omega experience, provides that orchestration, with pluggable runtime, storage and networking. The cost is learning and operating the cluster.

q: Plan how to evolve a three-tier on-premises web application (DNS, firewall, load-balanced web and app tiers, active-passive database) to a cloud-native architecture in stages. For each stage, say what it gains and what triggers the next one.
a: Stage 1, one-to-one mapping: managed DNS, CDN at the edge, cloud load balancers, VMs or containers for the tiers and a managed database. This gains managed operations and possibly autoscaling, with little application change. Stage 2, containerise the tiers and run replicas behind Kubernetes Services with images in a registry and IaC for everything. The trigger is a need for faster, repeatable deployments. Stage 3, extract business capabilities as services behind an API gateway, with a mesh for internal traffic, only where independent delivery or scaling is a real problem. Functions are added for event-driven parts. Each stage adds operational complexity, so take the next one only when its trigger appears.

q: For a new system with a 24/7 order API, a nightly reconciliation job and an image-thumbnail task triggered by uploads, compare VMs, containers and functions, and choose one for each component.
a: VMs include a guest OS and give OS control, containers share a kernel and package dependencies lightly, and functions run on demand with a managed runtime. Order API: containers for always-on load and portability. Nightly reconciliation: a scheduled container job, or a function if it fits execution limits. Thumbnails: functions, for short, sporadic, event-triggered work billed per invocation. Choose by duration, startup latency, state, runtime control and cost, not by packaging fashion.

q: You are asked to produce the architecture for a new cloud-native platform. Using the Day 1 framing (what, how, where, and two audiences), outline what the deliverable must contain and how you would keep it from going stale.
a: What: a reference architecture with layers, components and how they interact. How: decisions with the constraints, requirements and objectives behind each. Where: data, infrastructure, application, platform, security and enterprise viewpoints. Deliver diagrams for people and IaC, YAML and config for machines, so the running system is generated from the architecture. Keep functional and non-functional requirements and recorded technical debt in the backlog. Because the IaC is part of the architecture, changes to it go through review, which keeps the design and the system aligned.

q: An app moves from one server to 6 load-balanced instances in the cloud, and users start losing their shopping carts between requests. What changed in the persistence problem?
a: Each instance was keeping cart state locally, which worked with one server but fails when requests land on different instances. In a distributed deployment you must decide which state is shared, where it lives and how it survives an instance failure. Moving carts to a shared store fixes it, at the cost of a network call per request and a new component that must be available.

q: A team starting a new cloud app with modest load plans four different databases from day one 'because that's cloud-native'. Do you agree?
a: No. Cloud deployment makes data distribution an explicit choice, not a requirement to use many stores. A single managed relational database may be enough at first. Add stores, partitioning or replication when access patterns, scale or availability requirements justify the extra operational complexity.

q: A legacy hierarchical database makes a new 'all orders for product X across customers' report very slow, because data is reached from customer records down. Why does the relational model help here?
a: Navigational models tie access to the physical tree, so a query that doesn't follow the parent-child path has to traverse everything. The relational model separates how data is presented from how it is stored, so the same normalised tables can be joined in whatever direction a new query needs. The cost is join work at query time.

q: A team wants an object database because 'mapping our class hierarchy to tables is painful'. What does history suggest, and what would you propose?
a: Object databases did address the object-relational mismatch, but they never won market share, and ORM tools solved much of the mismatch on top of mature relational databases, for example by flattening an inheritance hierarchy into one table with a type column. Propose an ORM over a relational database, or a document store if the objects really are self-contained aggregates.

q: A finance system needs precise reporting, star schemas and strict integrity, and is expected to grow tenfold in 5 years. Is a relational database still a sound choice?
a: Yes for the requirements: it is mature and precise, with normalisation, ACID and SQL for reporting. The risk is its main weakness, being expensive to scale for very large distributed workloads. Plan for that growth (bigger instances, read replicas, partitioning, or NewSQL later) rather than giving up integrity now.

q: Using the search example from the lecture, explain why a relational database was a poor fit for a keyword-to-URL lookup at web scale.
a: The workload is a huge, read-mostly lookup spread across many servers, with no need for multi-record transactions, many entities or integrity constraints. A relational database would provide features the workload doesn't use while making the distribution it does need costly. Where joins and transactions matter, the balance reverses.

q: An IoT platform ingests 50,000 sensor readings a second, and each device type sends a different set of fields. Which of the V's are causing pressure, and what do they point to?
a: Velocity (real-time ingestion needs distributed persistence for throughput), Volume (scale out on commodity or cloud servers, not one big server) and Variety (fields differ by device, so a non-static schema helps). Together they point to a distributed NoSQL store for the raw readings. Keep any transactional data, such as billing, wherever its integrity needs are best met.

q: A 5-person team proposes a graph database, a document store, a cache and a relational database for an app with 2,000 users. When is polyglot persistence a bad idea, and what would you do?
a: When the gain from a better storage fit is smaller than the cost of programming and operating each extra technology, which is likely here given the team size and load. Start with fewer stores, add one only when an access pattern clearly needs it, and wrap data access in services so a later change has limited impact.

q: Invoices are always read and written as a whole, with header and line items together, and the format varies by country. Document store or normalised relational tables?
a: A document store: each invoice is a natural aggregate that maps to one document, so reads need no joins and the varying fields don't need schema changes. You give up easy cross-invoice constraints and ad-hoc joins, for example reporting across customers and products, which may need a separate reporting store.

q: A social app's 'people you may know' query joins the friendships table to itself three levels deep and is slow. Which pattern fits, and what should you check before switching?
a: A graph store, because the question is relationship traversal across nodes and edges rather than repeated joins. Check that the real workload is traversal-heavy and benchmark it with realistic data and indexes; graph stores are not universally faster than joins. Keep other data, such as profiles, in whatever store suits it.

q: In a column-family store, customer rows have a profile family and an order-history family. A screen reads only the profile. Why does the grouping matter?
a: Columns in a family are assumed to be read together and are stored together, so reading the profile doesn't pull the large order history. Rows can stay sparse, since customers without orders cost nothing. Choose families from the access patterns, because a screen that needs both families in one read loses this benefit.

q: A game needs a real-time global leaderboard updated thousands of times a second. Which store type fits, and what would you keep elsewhere?
a: An in-memory key-value store with sorted structures such as rankings, because a leaderboard is direct keyed access that must be very fast. Keep durable data such as player accounts and purchases in a durable store, since a cache can lose data on failure unless persistence is configured.

q: A team picks a column-family store because 'we'll have terabytes of data'. Is size a good reason, and what should decide it?
a: No. Data size alone doesn't decide the store family. Decide from the queries and update patterns: column-family for row-key access to large sparse records grouped into families, documents for nested aggregates, relational for joins and constraints. Model the access patterns, then benchmark the real queries.

q: A payments company needs SQL, strong ACID transactions and horizontal scale across regions. Is NewSQL the obvious answer?
a: It is a candidate, because NewSQL aims to combine relational and SQL semantics with distributed scale. Evaluate the coordination cost: distributed guarantees add latency, especially across regions. Compare it with a sharded relational design and with NoSQL products that offer transactions at the scope you need.

q: An analyst asks to run sales reports on the operational column-family store 'because both are columnar, like the warehouse'. What is the misunderstanding?
a: A column-family store groups sparse, row-keyed records for operational access. An analytical columnar warehouse is a SQL store built for large scans and aggregations. They solve different workloads, so heavy reports on the operational store would perform poorly and compete with live traffic. Feed a warehouse for analytics instead.

q: An app is overwhelmed by writes. A teammate proposes adding read replicas with master-slave replication. Will it help? What would?
a: No. Replicas add read capacity, but every write still goes to the single leader, so the write bottleneck stays. Shard by a suitable key so independent writes go to different servers. Peer-to-peer replication may help some workloads, but each update still has to propagate and may need conflict handling.

q: A regional retailer stores Singapore and Malaysia orders together and has one global product list. How would you distribute each kind of data?
a: Shard orders by country so each node handles its own reads and writes, spreading both volume and write load. Replicate the product list to every node, because it is read-heavy and shared, and single-leader replication fits since writes are rare. Cross-country reports now need to query several shards.

q: A bank's product team wants eventual consistency 'everywhere, for scale'. Where would you allow it and where not?
a: Keep authoritative balances and transfers transactional (ACID), because temporarily inconsistent balances are wrong and costly. Allow eventual consistency (BASE) for derived views such as an activity feed, analytics or a product listing, where a briefly stale read does little harm. State the consistency requirement per operation instead of setting one policy for the whole system.

q: After switching to peer-to-peer replication, two regions accept conflicting updates to the same customer record during a network split. What caused this, and what are the options?
a: Multiple writers with asynchronous propagation favour availability, so both regions accepted writes and the copies diverged. Options are a conflict-resolution rule such as last-writer-wins or merging, routing each record's writes to a home region, or coordinated writes for that data, which cost latency and availability during a split.

q: A load-balanced web fleet must share user-uploaded files between instances. Which storage fits, and why not a block volume attached to one VM?
a: A network file system if the app needs shared file semantics, or object storage if it can use object APIs, which also lets web and mobile clients fetch the files. A block volume is normally a disk for one attached VM, not a shared filesystem, and concurrent writers need explicit support and coordination.

q: A team stores its database files on the VM's local instance disk because it is fastest. What is the risk, and what would you change?
a: Instance-store disk is ephemeral: data can disappear on stop, termination or host failure. Put database files on a persistent block volume with suitable retention and backups, or use a managed database. Keep local disk for scratch data that can be regenerated.

q: Images must be served to a web app, a mobile app and a partner's batch job. Why is object storage the natural fit?
a: Object storage is reached through a standard web API, so every channel and service model uses it the same way without mounting a disk. It is also the most flexible and widely used option. The trade-off is that it isn't a normal filesystem, so apps that expect file locking or in-place edits need changes.

q: A team wants to install a database on a VM instead of using the provider's managed relational database 'to keep control'. When is that justified?
a: When compatibility, a needed extension or version, or a capability missing from the managed option justifies the operating burden. Otherwise managed is the better default: it offloads much maintenance, patching, backup and availability work. Either way, the customer still designs access, schemas, capacity and recovery.

q: An e-commerce app needs a session cache, a catalogue with varying product attributes, sales analytics and 'customers who bought this also bought' recommendations. Match each to a store type and give the reason.
a: Session cache: in-memory key-value, because it is fast keyed access to disposable data. Catalogue: document or key-value, because attributes vary per product and items are read whole. Analytics: a columnar SQL warehouse for scans and aggregations. Recommendations: a graph store for relationship traversal. Each extra store adds operational cost, so drop one if a simpler store meets the need.

q: Design the persistence strategy for a cloud-native e-commerce platform with a catalogue (varying attributes), carts that must survive a cache failure, orders, recommendations and product images. Justify each store and say which one you would drop if the team were only 4 people.
a: Orders: a managed relational database for ACID transactions. Catalogue: a document store for flexible attributes read as whole items. Carts: a durable key-value store, or the relational database, with a cache in front, since carts must survive cache loss. Recommendations: a graph store for traversal. Images: object storage served through a CDN. With 4 people, drop the graph store and compute recommendations in batch from the order database, and consider keeping the catalogue relational, because each extra store adds programming and operational complexity.

q: A regional retailer's single relational database can't keep up with growing order writes across Singapore and Malaysia. A teammate proposes read replicas. Evaluate that, then propose how to scale the data tier and name two side effects to monitor.
a: Read replicas won't fix a write bottleneck, because all writes still go to one leader. Shard orders by country so each node serves its own reads and writes, and replicate the shared, read-heavy product list to both nodes with single-leader replication. Keep payment data under ACID and accept eventual consistency only where the business allows. Monitor replica lag on the product list (stale prices) and cross-shard query cost for regional reports.

q: Recommend data stores for a global banking ledger and for a social media status feed, and explain why the SQL versus NoSQL label alone doesn't settle the choice.
a: The ledger needs transactional invariants and durability, so a relational or NewSQL store fits, weighing distributed coordination cost against scale needs. The feed tolerates briefly stale replicas and needs high write and read scale, so a distributed NoSQL store with eventual consistency fits. The label doesn't settle it, because NoSQL products vary in transaction scope and relational systems can distribute. Decide from per-operation consistency requirements, access patterns and coordination cost.

q: A manager says 'NoSQL replaced relational databases, so all new systems should be NoSQL.' Using the V's of big data and the web-search example, explain why NoSQL emerged and argue whether the claim holds.
a: NoSQL emerged because variety needed flexible schemas, volume needed scale-out on commodity servers, and velocity needed distributed throughput. The web-search lookup needed none of the joins or multi-record transactions that relational systems provide. The claim doesn't hold: relational databases remain the natural fit for constraints, joins and ACID transactions. Polyglot persistence uses each model where it fits and accepts the complexity only when the benefit is larger.

q: An image-processing service has 10 worker VMs. Choose storage for temporary processing scratch space, the job database's data files, configuration shared by all workers, and finished images served to web and mobile apps. Then say what breaks if the shared configuration is put on one VM's block volume.
a: Scratch: ephemeral instance disk, since it can be regenerated. Database files: a persistent block volume with retention and backups, or a managed database. Shared configuration: a network file system. Finished images: object storage reached through its API by both apps. A block volume is normally attached to one VM, so the other 9 workers couldn't read the configuration, and that VM's failure would take the configuration with it.

q: A company moved its app onto Kubernetes on a public cloud, but releases still happen quarterly by hand and nobody watches metrics. Is it cloud native? Use the three Ps.
a: Only on the Platforms P. The Properties (observable, resilient, loosely coupled) and the Practices (automation, continuous delivery, DevOps) are missing, so it gets little of the speed, resilience or scale that cloud native aims for. Add CI/CD, monitoring and automated recovery before calling it cloud native.

q: A team says 'we use only open-standard containers, so we have no lock-in.' Do you agree?
a: Partly. Open standards make tools easier to integrate and can lower switching costs, but lock-in also comes from provider-specific APIs, managed data services and operational dependencies. Check each managed service the app uses, and how its data would move, before claiming portability.

q: During a zone failure, an app's autoscaler added capacity but users still saw errors for 20 minutes. Which cloud-native property was missing, and why isn't autoscaling enough?
a: Resilience: the ability to continue or recover after failure. Autoscaling adjusts capacity to demand, but it doesn't reroute traffic around a failed zone or replace dependencies that went down with it. Resilience needs design work such as multi-zone placement, health checks, failover and bounded retries.

q: A new service processes uploaded documents within seconds of arrival, runs a few hundred times a day, and needs no special runtime. Another holds long-lived WebSocket connections. CaaS or FaaS for each?
a: FaaS for the document processor: short, event-driven work, where the platform handles runtime and autoscaling and you pay only when it runs. CaaS for the WebSocket service, which is long-running and needs runtime control, something functions handle poorly. FaaS gives up control and portability; CaaS keeps them but you operate more.

q: A team chose managed Kubernetes and says they no longer have any infrastructure work. Is that right?
a: Not necessarily. CaaS manages the container platform components, but depending on the offering, worker-node operations such as patching and scaling may still fall to the customer, and data accountability always stays with the customer. Check the provider's actual responsibility split. 'Favour managed services' moves effort to business code but doesn't remove all operations.

q: A container image passed every test in staging but fails in production with the same image tag. What is the most likely cause?
a: The image fixes the app and dependency versions, but behaviour also depends on external configuration, platform features and backing services, which differ between staging and production. Compare environment config, secrets, service endpoints and platform versions. Keeping dev and prod sufficiently alike reduces this.

q: A web tier uses sticky sessions with session data held in instance memory. During a scale-in event, users are logged out. Diagnose it and fix it.
a: Scale-in removed instances that held the only copy of some sessions, so sticky routing sent users to sessions that no longer existed. Move session state to a shared store, or use suitable client-held tokens, so any ready instance can serve the next request. The cost is a shared store on the request path that must itself be available.

q: A team runs a database in Kubernetes with a StatefulSet. A reviewer suggests a managed external database instead. When is each right?
a: An external managed database is usually the better default: the provider handles backups, replication and patching, and the cluster stays stateless. A StatefulSet, or an Operator that encodes operational knowledge, is right when the store must run in the cluster for control or portability, and the team accepts operating it.

q: A teammate says 'we're on containers, so our servers are cattle now.' What would show whether that is true?
a: Pets versus cattle is an operating model, not a technology. Check whether any instance can be deleted and recreated from automation without losing data or needing someone to fix it by hand. Containers that are patched in place or hold unique local state are still pets. Disposable VMs can be cattle.

q: A team rebuilds the image separately for test and for production with different config baked in. Which factors does this break, and what is the risk?
a: It breaks build/release/run separation and config in the environment. The production artifact is not the one that was tested, so builds can drift through dependency or build differences. Build one immutable artifact, combine it with environment config at release, and promote the same artifact. A rollback still needs compatible config and schema state.

q: An autoscaler adds instances during a spike, but each takes 3 minutes to start and loses in-flight work when removed. Which factors are failing, and why do they matter together?
a: Disposability (fast start, graceful stop) and probably stateless processes. Concurrency through scale-out only works if the platform can add and remove processes freely; slow starts mean capacity arrives after the spike, and abrupt stops lose work. Speed up startup, handle termination signals to finish or hand back work, and keep state in backing services.
