q: After an incident, engineers can't find the logs because the failed containers were already replaced. Which factor was ignored, and what is the fix?
a: Logs as event streams. Instances are disposable, so local log files vanish with them. Write logs to stdout as a stream and have the platform ship them to a central aggregator that can be searched across all instances. The cost is running or paying for the log pipeline and its storage.

q: A team puts its database password in an environment variable and calls it 'secure because it's not in the code'. Do you agree?
a: Not fully. Externalising config is right, because one artifact then serves several environments, but an environment variable alone doesn't protect a secret: it can leak through logs, dumps or anyone with access to the deployment spec. Source it from protected secret storage with restricted access and inject it at runtime.

q: Someone deletes a pod by mistake and it comes back a few seconds later. Explain why, and say what this means for how you change production.
a: The manifest declares a desired state (for example 3 replicas), and the control plane continuously reconciles the cluster to it, so it recreated the pod. Change production by changing the declared state, not by editing live resources, because reconciliation will undo manual fixes. This is also what gives self-healing.

q: A platform has 25 internal services with inconsistent retry and encryption behaviour, plus a public mobile API. Where do an API gateway and a service mesh each fit?
a: The gateway is the entry point for the mobile clients' external traffic (routing, authentication, rate limits). The mesh manages the 25 services' internal traffic, adding consistent routing, resilience, observability and encryption without changing service code. Both have a control plane and a data plane. The mesh adds operating cost, which is justified here by the inconsistency across 25 services.

q: A legacy app has been containerised but still writes to local disk and uses sticky sessions. Where is it on the maturity model, and what is the next step?
a: Not yet Cloud Ready, which requires no permanent disk access and a self-contained app using platform-managed backing services. Move files and sessions to backing services first. Then adopt the 12 factors and horizontal scaling to reach Cloud Friendly. Containerising alone doesn't move it up the ladder.

q: An app is 12-factor and scales horizontally on platform HA, and a team wants to call it 'cloud native'. What would it still need?
a: That is Cloud Friendly. Cloud Resilient adds fault tolerance, a cloud-agnostic runtime, bundled metrics and proactive failure testing. Cloud Native adds microservices and API-first design. Whether to go further depends on whether the business needs independent deployability and resilience that justify the cost.

q: A company adopted containers and microservices but kept separate dev and ops teams with handoffs, and releases are still slow. Why?
a: Short continuous delivery and fast recovery need collaborating teams and automation as well as the technical properties. Handoffs between silos keep the release cycle long, whatever the architecture. Pair the architecture with DevOps practices and shared ownership, or the speed-to-market benefit won't appear.

q: Business rules for loan approval call the database driver and the web framework directly. The team now wants to change databases and unit-test the rules. What is the problem, and what would you change?
a: The rules are coupled to the database and framework, so changing either means rewriting logic, and tests need a real database. Separate concerns: put the rules in code that is independent of frameworks, UI, database and external agencies, and reach the database through an interface. The cost is an extra layer of abstraction.

q: Two projects are choosing a cloud: migrating a legacy enterprise app with on-premises integrations, and building a new consumer product. Which characteristics should weigh most for each?
a: The legacy migration should weigh ease of migration, backward compatibility, integration with the internal network and data location most. The new product should weigh productivity, elasticity, use-based pricing and a rich managed-service portfolio. The same provider can win for one project and lose for the other, so start from each project's goal.

q: A checkout request needs an API service, a payment service and a database in series, each at 99.9% availability. A manager promises 99.9% end-to-end. Is that realistic?
a: No. For independent components in series, availability multiplies: 0.999 × 0.999 × 0.999 ≈ 99.7%, so the path is less available than any single part. This is an estimate, since shared failure modes and redundancy change it. To reach 99.9%, add redundancy or failover on the critical path, or reduce dependencies the request needs.

q: Order submissions spike tenfold at sale start, and the order processor falls over. How do queues help, and what must the consumers guarantee?
a: Put a queue between submission and processing so producers aren't blocked, the backlog levels the peak, and competing consumers scale out to drain it. If a consumer fails, the message is delivered again, so processing must be idempotent to avoid duplicate orders. Users now get 'accepted' rather than 'completed' immediately.

q: The primary database is replicated to a second region, so the team drops nightly backups. What risk does this create?
a: Replication copies an accidental delete or a corrupting update to every replica, so there's nothing earlier to recover. Backups keep recoverable earlier states. Keep backups, test restores against acceptable data loss and recovery time, and make replay idempotent.

q: Customer data must stay in Singapore. The app's database is in Singapore, but failover is to another country's region and metrics go to a global monitoring service. Is the design compliant?
a: Probably not. Data protection rules apply to every copy, including failover replicas and any customer data inside metrics or logs. Choose an in-country failover location, or confirm the rules allow it, and scrub personal data from telemetry or keep it in-region. The cost may be weaker DR options.

q: A retailer's monolithic web shop loses customers' carts whenever a server crashes and can't cope with sale-day spikes of 20 times normal traffic. Diagnose the causes and propose a cloud native redesign, naming one new risk it introduces.
a: The diagnosis: sticky sessions and in-memory carts make servers pets, and the single scaling unit can't grow fast enough. Make the web tier stateless with carts in a shared store or managed database, split hot areas such as checkout into services behind an API gateway, run them as containers with horizontal autoscaling, and put order processing behind a queue to level peaks. Apply 12-factor practices and CI/CD. The new risks are distributed failures and eventual consistency between services, so add observability, timeouts and idempotent consumers.

q: Audit this service against the 12 factors: config is baked into images per environment, logs go to local files, the service takes 4 minutes to start, it writes uploads to local disk, and a database migration runs at every container start. Rank the gaps by operational risk and give the fix for each.
a: Highest risk: uploads on local disk (breaks stateless processes, so data is lost when instances are replaced); move them to object storage. Next, per-environment images (breaks build/release/run and config), meaning the tested artifact isn't the one deployed; build once and inject config at release, with secrets from protected storage. Then the 4-minute start (disposability), which defeats autoscaling. Then the migration at startup, which should be a one-off admin process to avoid concurrent migrations. Finally local logs, which vanish; stream them to an aggregator.

q: You must offer 99.95% availability for a service whose request path uses a gateway, a compute tier and a managed database, each with a 99.9% SLA. Explain why the target is at risk and propose design changes, with the cost of each.
a: In series, 0.999³ ≈ 99.7%, below the target, and provider SLAs alone can't guarantee the end-to-end figure. Add redundancy on the path: compute across zones behind health-checked load balancing, a database with a synchronous standby, and possibly a second region for the most critical path. Remove dependencies from the synchronous path using queues and caches. Bound retries and use circuit breakers so one slow dependency doesn't cascade. Each step adds cost and complexity, so check feasibility: if the budget or skills can't support it, renegotiate the SLA.

q: A bank's 20-year-old core app is released twice a year, runs on large VMs sized for peak, and is owned by separate dev and ops teams. A new digital-banking team wants weekly releases. Contrast the traditional and cloud-native approaches for each part, and say whether the core app should be converted.
a: Traditional: long release cycles, siloed teams, a tightly coupled monolith and server-centric vertical capacity pre-provisioned for peak. Cloud native: continuous delivery, DevOps teams, loosely coupled API-based services, and disposable, horizontally scaled containers. The digital team should build cloud native. The core app doesn't need to convert all at once: expose it through APIs and modernise where business drivers justify it, because these are tendencies and the core app can adopt automation and DevOps without a rewrite.

q: You run 30 microservices on Kubernetes across dev, test and prod. Secrets are in plain manifests, retries differ per team, and an outage last month cascaded through internal calls. Propose how to manage configuration, secrets and service-to-service traffic.
a: Keep ordinary config outside the image and per environment, so the same artifact is promoted through all three. Move secrets to protected secret storage with restricted access and inject them at runtime, because plain manifests or environment variables alone aren't protection. Declare everything in version-controlled manifests so the control plane reconciles drift. With 30 services and a cascading outage, a service mesh is justified for consistent timeouts, bounded retries, circuit breaking, encryption and tracing without code changes, with an API gateway for external traffic. The mesh adds operational overhead and latency to manage.

q: A release is rolled back by redeploying the previous image, but the app still fails. Why didn't image immutability make the rollback safe?
a: An immutable image restores the old application code exactly, but behaviour also depends on configuration and external data. If the new release ran a database migration the old code can't handle, a code-only rollback fails. Make schema changes backward-compatible, or plan a data recovery step alongside image rollbacks.

q: A team chose Kubernetes expecting it to give them a database, a message queue and logging out of the box, like their old PaaS. What do you tell them?
a: Kubernetes is not a PaaS. It schedules, heals, scales and networks containers, but it supplies no databases, queues, service marketplace or built-in logging stack. They must choose and integrate those, for example as managed services, or adopt a platform built on Kubernetes that adds them. The upside is freedom of language and framework.

q: A team turned on autoscaling in Kubernetes, but pods never scale during load spikes. What is likely missing?
a: Autoscaling needs metrics and a policy: a metrics source, resource requests or target metrics, and an autoscaler configured with sensible thresholds. Spare node capacity is also needed for new pods to be placed. Declaring replicas alone keeps a fixed count; Kubernetes only automates what has been configured.

q: A 3-person team runs 4 services on Docker Compose today and asks whether to move to Swarm or Kubernetes. What would you recommend, and what decides it?
a: Swarm is simpler and reuses their Compose files, which suits a small, stable Docker estate. Kubernetes has richer objects (Deployments, Services, Ingress, volumes, namespaces), managed offerings on every major cloud and a larger ecosystem, which matters if they expect to grow or need portability. The trade-off is learning and operating cost versus capability and future flexibility.

q: An organisation already runs big-data frameworks on a shared cluster and wants to add container scheduling. How do the Mesos and Kubernetes models differ for this?
a: Mesos is a general resource manager that offers cluster resources to frameworks, with Marathon doing container scheduling as one framework among others such as data-processing ones. Kubernetes builds its own scheduler and controllers into the control plane and focuses on container workloads. Mesos fits sharing one cluster across heterogeneous frameworks; Kubernetes gives a more integrated container platform.

q: You apply a Deployment with 3 replicas, and the pods stay 'Pending'. Trace where in the reconcile chain things stopped, and the likely cause.
a: The API server stored the spec in etcd, and the controller created pod objects, which is why they exist as Pending. The scheduler has not assigned them to nodes, most likely because no node has enough free resources for their requests or none matches their constraints. Check scheduling events, node capacity and the pod's resource requests.

q: A team runs a self-managed cluster with a single etcd member and no backups. What is the risk?
a: etcd holds all cluster state and configuration. Losing it means the control plane no longer knows desired or current state, and the cluster can't be managed or rebuilt as it was. Run etcd replicated across failure domains and back it up regularly. A managed control plane shifts this duty to the provider.

q: Pods on one node are running and healthy, but traffic sent to their Service never reaches them from other nodes. Which node component would you suspect first, and why not kubelet?
a: kube-proxy, which programs the network rules that route Service traffic to pod endpoints. kubelet manages pod and container lifecycles, and the pods are running, so it is doing its job. Also check that the Service's selector matches the pod labels, because a mismatch gives the same symptom.

q: A team puts its web app, a log shipper, and the reporting service it calls into the same pod 'to keep things together'. Which belong together, and why?
a: The web app and the log shipper: the shipper is a tightly coupled helper that shares the app's lifecycle and storage. The reporting service should be its own pod, because containers in a pod share a node, IP and lifecycle, so they scale and fail together, and the reporting service needs to scale and update independently.

q: A frontend calls a backend by a pod IP copied from the console, and it breaks every few days. Why, and what is the fix?
a: Pods are ephemeral: they get new IPs when replaced or rescheduled. Put a Service in front of the backend pods. It gives a stable IP and DNS name and load-balances across whichever ready pods match its label selector.

q: Three web services must share one public domain with paths /shop, /blog and /api. Would you expose each Service directly or use an Ingress?
a: An Ingress: one external entry point with path-based routing to the three Services. Exposing each directly needs three external endpoints and gives no shared host or path routing. An Ingress needs an installed controller to implement its rules, which is one more component to run.

q: Two teams share a cluster in separate Namespaces, and a security review assumes their traffic is isolated. Is it?
a: No. Namespaces organise and scope resources but don't restrict traffic by themselves. Add NetworkPolicies (with a network plugin that supports them) to limit pod-to-pod traffic, RBAC to limit API access, and ResourceQuotas to stop one team starving the other.

q: A startup's production cluster is a single-node local setup like the one used in the lecture labs, because 'it works fine'. What would you tell them?
a: One machine is one failure domain: a host failure or upgrade takes everything down, and that setup is designed for learning and testing, not HA. Move to a managed or properly designed self-managed cluster with multiple nodes across zones, and test node and control-plane recovery.

q: A Deployment is applied but reports 0 of 3 pods available, even though pods with the app are running. What would you check first?
a: That the selector's matchLabels match the pod template's labels. The Deployment finds and counts its pods by label, so a mismatch means it can't track the pods it should own. Also check that the Service selector uses the same labels so traffic reaches them.

q: A team changed a value in a ConfigMap, but the app still uses the old value an hour later. Why, and what are the options?
a: The ConfigMap separates config from the image, but the running process may only read config at startup, and environment variables taken from a ConfigMap are not refreshed. Restart the pods through a rolling update, or mount the ConfigMap as a file and add reload logic. Sensitive values belong in Secrets with access and encryption controls.

q: Self-managed Kubernetes or a managed Kubernetes service for a team of 4 running 15 services? What should decide it?
a: Managed is the likely choice: the provider operates selected platform components, such as the control plane, so the small team avoids upgrades and control-plane recovery. Self-managed gives more control but leaves all cluster operations to the team. With either option, check the responsibility boundary: worker capacity, workload security and application availability still need the team's design.

q: A cluster spans three zones in one region. A manager says the app is now 'resilient to anything'. What does it cover and what doesn't it?
a: Spreading replicas across zones covers the loss of a node or a zone, provided placement and spare capacity are configured. It doesn't cover a regional outage or a control-plane failure in that region. Regional resilience needs multiple clusters plus explicit traffic failover and data recovery design.

q: Map a stateless API, a nightly report, a per-node log collector and a database onto Kubernetes objects. Justify each.
a: Stateless API: a Deployment with several replicas behind a Service, because it scales freely. Nightly report: a CronJob, for scheduled batch work. Log collector: a DaemonSet, so one runs on every node. Database: a StatefulSet with PVCs, or a managed external database, which is usually the better default because the provider handles backups, replication and patching.

q: A compromised pod in one namespace could call the payment service and consumed all cluster CPU. Which objects around the workload would have limited this?
a: A NetworkPolicy restricting who can reach the payment service, a ResourceQuota capping the namespace's consumption (with resource limits on pods), and a dedicated ServiceAccount with only the permissions the workload needs. These are configured controls: Kubernetes supplies them, but they are off unless you set them.

q: An API pod's liveness probe calls the database. During a 5-minute database slowdown, every API pod restarts repeatedly. What went wrong, and how should the probes be set?
a: Liveness failed because of a dependency, so restarts couldn't fix it and they added load during recovery. Liveness should detect only a process that needs a restart, such as a deadlock. Readiness should decide whether the pod can serve traffic, so dependency checks belong there, if anywhere.

q: Before an app starts, its database schema must be migrated, and throughout its life its logs must be shipped to a central store. Which pattern fits each?
a: An init container for the migration, because it runs to completion before the app container starts. A sidecar for log shipping, because it runs alongside the app for the pod's whole life and shares its storage. Neither requires changing the app's code. Make the migration safe to run more than once, because pods restart.

q: A stateful service writes data to its container filesystem, and the data disappears after a node failure. What is the fix, and what does a pod-level volume not solve?
a: A container's filesystem lives and dies with the container. Use a PersistentVolumeClaim bound to a PersistentVolume so the data outlives the pod, and a replacement pod can remount it. A pod-level volume lets containers in the same pod share files, but it is still tied to the pod's lifetime.

q: One of three replicas crashes during peak load and users see errors for a minute. Explain which mechanisms recover it, and why errors still happened.
a: Readiness removes the failed pod from Service endpoints, kubelet restarts a crashed container, and the controller replaces a lost pod. Errors still happen if requests were in flight, if the 2 remaining replicas lack the capacity for peak load, or if there was no spare node capacity for a replacement. None of these mechanisms guarantees zero downtime without headroom and graceful shutdown.

q: A retailer's monolith has outages during sales peaks that are 15 times normal traffic. Propose a Kubernetes-based design, justify the main objects you would use, and say what Kubernetes will not solve for you.
a: Split the parts that peak, such as catalogue and checkout, into Deployments with several ready replicas spread across zones, Services for stable discovery, and an Ingress with an installed controller for external HTTP routing. Add autoscaling with metrics, resource requests and node headroom. Externalise state to a managed database and shared cache, and use readiness probes, graceful shutdown and rolling updates for deployments. Kubernetes won't supply the database, queue or monitoring stack, won't guarantee zero downtime without spare capacity, and won't fix a data tier that can't take the peak.

q: A new node joins a cluster and someone deletes a pod by accident at the same moment. Explain, component by component, how the control plane and nodes return the system to its desired state, and which single component's loss would be most serious.
a: The API server is the only entry point and records changes in etcd. The controller manager sees fewer replicas than declared and creates a replacement pod object. The scheduler places it on a node with capacity, possibly the new one. That node's kubelet starts it through the container runtime, and kube-proxy updates Service routing so traffic reaches it. Losing etcd would be most serious, because it holds all desired and current state, so it should be replicated and backed up.

q: Design the external access path for three web microservices (/products, /orders, /payments) under one domain. Explain the role of each object, and say what changes if /payments must be reachable only from the orders service internally.
a: Create a Deployment and a Service for each microservice, with selectors that match the pod labels, and one Ingress with path rules routing to the three Services, implemented by an installed Ingress controller. Services give stable backends, and the controller handles external HTTP routing. If /payments must be internal only, remove it from the Ingress, keep its Service internal, and add a NetworkPolicy that allows traffic only from the orders pods.

q: An organisation is choosing between a local single-node cluster, self-managed Kubernetes and a managed Kubernetes service for development and production of 20 services, with a 5-person platform team. Recommend a setup for each environment and justify it.
a: Use a local single-node cluster for developer learning and testing only. For production, use managed Kubernetes: the provider runs selected platform components such as the control plane, so the small team avoids upgrades and control-plane recovery. Self-managed would give more control but leave all cluster operations to 5 people. Check the provider's responsibility boundary, since worker capacity, workload security and application availability still need design, and plan multiple zones for production.

q: A team's Kubernetes design keeps database credentials in a ConfigMap, runs its database as a single pod with data on the container filesystem, and puts every team in one Namespace with no quotas. Critique the design and give corrected choices.
a: Credentials in a ConfigMap aren't protected, so move them to Secrets with access and encryption controls, or to an external secret store. A database writing to its container filesystem loses data when the pod is replaced, so use a StatefulSet with PVCs, or preferably a managed database. One shared Namespace without quotas gives no governance, so give each team its own Namespace with RBAC, ResourceQuotas and NetworkPolicies. Keep services stateless so they scale as Deployments, and use one image per release with config injected per environment.

q: A CIO wants to pick the provider ranked highest in an analyst's Magic Quadrant and stop there. What does the ranking tell you, and what does it not?
a: It gives an independent view of vendor viability and capability using weighted criteria such as overall viability, market responsiveness and product strength. It doesn't tell you whether the vendor fits this workload. Also check the regions you need, pricing, your team's skills and how specific services behave, and treat the ranking as one input among several.

q: On the same provider, a team must run (a) a long-running order API that may later move to another cloud and (b) an image-resize task triggered a few hundred times a day. Managed Kubernetes, FaaS or VMs for each?
a: (a) Managed Kubernetes: long-running containerised services keep their packaging and orchestration portable across clouds. (b) FaaS: short, event-driven, no servers to operate, and billed only per use at this volume. VMs would give the most control but the most to operate, which is justified only if a workload needs OS-level control.

q: Two providers both list a 'managed message queue'. A teammate says they are interchangeable, so switching later will be easy. Do you agree?
a: No. Providers offer overlapping building blocks, not identical semantics. Ordering, delivery guarantees, message size limits, access model, regions and operating boundaries can differ. State the capability you need, check each product against it, and keep provider-specific calls behind your own interface if switching is a real requirement.

q: A media company must store millions of uploaded videos and serve them to users worldwide. Object, block or file storage, and why not the others?
a: Object storage: it scales cheaply for large unstructured files, is reached over HTTP APIs, and suits media, backups and archives, ideally with a CDN for global delivery. Block storage is a low-latency disk for one VM and doesn't scale as shared media storage. File storage is a shared filesystem for VMs, which the web and mobile clients don't need.

q: A lift-and-shift app on 8 VMs expects a shared directory, and its database needs a fast local disk. Which storage type for each?
a: File storage for the shared directory, since many VMs can mount it without the app changing, which is typical for lift-and-shift. Block storage for the database disk, for low-latency attached volumes. Moving the shared directory to object storage later would scale better but needs code changes.

q: A web app behind a managed load balancer went down when its only zone failed, and an attack sent malformed HTTP requests that the network firewall didn't block. What was missing in each case?
a: A load balancer only helps availability if healthy backend capacity remains, so the backends needed to be spread across zones. Network firewall rules filter connections, not HTTP content, so a WAF was needed to filter malicious HTTP requests. Being managed doesn't mean configured: capacity, placement and filtering are still design choices.

q: An order event must be processed once by one of 10 worker instances, and also trigger an email, a loyalty update and an analytics record. Queue, pub/sub or both?
a: Both. A queue distributes the order work among competing workers so each order is handled by one. Pub/sub fans the event out to independent subscribers (email, loyalty, analytics), usually with one queue per consumer group. Delivery can repeat in either case, so consumers must be idempotent.

q: A queue redelivers a payment task after a worker times out, and the customer is charged twice. What is the fix, and why not simply ask for 'exactly-once' delivery?
a: Make the business operation idempotent, for example by recording a stable payment identifier with its result so a retry returns the recorded outcome instead of charging again. Redelivery after a timeout is normal in messaging, and you can't rely on once-only delivery to guarantee once-only business effects.

q: A team must replay the last 7 days of click events to rebuild a broken analytics view. Would a message queue or a stream suit this, and why?
a: A stream: it keeps ordered event data for a retention period, so consumers can reprocess and replay from an earlier point. A queue normally removes a message once it has been processed, so there would be nothing to replay. The cost of a stream is retention storage and managing consumer positions.

q: A team building on managed services plans to add monitoring, identity and encryption 'after launch'. Why is that risky, and what should be in place at launch?
a: Without identity management, access is likely too broad. Without managed key encryption, data protection depends on ad-hoc handling. Without monitoring, failures go unseen. Retrofitting each later is harder than defining them in IaC from day one. Use the provider's managed identity, key management and monitoring, provisioned through IaC, so they deploy consistently.

q: Map a cloud-native e-commerce architecture (product browsing, carts, orders, product images, order processing, notifications) onto categories of managed services on one provider, justifying each, and name the decision that most increases lock-in.
a: Managed DNS and a load balancer with a WAF at the edge. Managed Kubernetes for the long-running services and FaaS for event handlers such as image resizing. A managed relational database for orders (ACID) and a NoSQL store for carts and sessions. Object storage with a CDN for images. A queue for order processing and pub/sub for notifications. Add monitoring, IaC, identity management and key management so operations and security are built in. The biggest lock-in usually comes from proprietary data and messaging services, because data and semantics don't move as easily as container images.

q: A company plans to run on three major providers 'for portability'. Using the idea of overlapping building blocks, assess what will be portable and what will not, and recommend whether to proceed.
a: Compare by capability categories such as managed Kubernetes, object storage and messaging, then check each service's semantics, regions and limits. Containers on Kubernetes keep packaging and orchestration portable. Data, identity, networking and proprietary managed-service APIs are not portable and need separate migration and integration work. Proceed only if a concrete benefit (regulation, resilience against a provider, a best-of-breed service) outweighs the cost of tripled skills and operations. Otherwise use one provider with an exit strategy.

q: A team must choose storage for VM boot disks, a database's data files, shared engineering files mounted by 20 VMs, and 5 years of backup archives. Recommend a type for each, and say what happens if the team puts everything on block storage to keep things simple.
a: Block storage for boot disks and database files, for low-latency attached volumes. File storage for the shared engineering files, since many VMs must mount them. Object storage for the backup archives, because it is cheap and durable at scale. With everything on block storage, the shared files can't easily be mounted by 20 VMs, and archives would cost much more than on object storage.

q: A CTO says: 'Use managed services everywhere, so availability and security are the provider's job.' Argue for and against, and state what remains the team's responsibility.
a: For: managed services offload patching, scaling, backups and much availability work, so teams can spend their effort on business code. Against: they increase lock-in through proprietary APIs, can cost more at scale, and tie you to the provider's SLA, which doesn't by itself meet an application SLA. The team still chooses capacity and availability options such as multi-zone placement, configures identity, permissions, encryption and retention, designs idempotent messaging, and tests recovery. Limit lock-in with open standards where it matters and keep an exit strategy.

q: A team's code is well structured, but releases take two weeks because deployments are manual and the app runs on hand-built VMs. A teammate says 'architecture is about the code, the platform is ops' business'. Do you agree?
a: No. In a cloud native full stack, the platform is part of the design: packaging as containers or functions and delivering through Git-driven pipelines shapes scalability and delivery speed as much as the code does. Here the platform is the bottleneck. Moving to automated pipelines and a container or function platform would cut the two-week cycle more than refactoring code would.

q: A manager reads that AI-assisted engineering will soon make teams smaller and work 'specification-driven', and proposes cutting architecture reviews because 'the AI writes the code'. How do you respond?
a: The lecture presents these as forecasts, not settled facts. Even if they come true, specifications and architectural constraints become the main input to AI-generated code, so clear quality attributes, review and verification matter more, not less. Cutting reviews removes the check on whether the generated code meets the constraints.

q: A retailer wants a mobile shopping experience launched within 2 months, on a small budget, and found through search engines. PWA or native?
a: A PWA: one web codebase, instant server-side updates, broad reach and search discoverability fit the deadline and budget. Check that the features it needs, such as push notifications and offline cart viewing, work on the target browsers. Native would only be justified if a required capability couldn't be delivered on the web.

q: Field inspectors must work for hours without signal, capture photos and read a Bluetooth sensor, and the app must be in the app stores. Native (or cross-platform native) or a PWA, and what does the choice mean for the backend?
a: Cross-platform native: deep hardware access (Bluetooth, camera), long offline operation with local storage and app-store presence point there, and browser support for these features varies. On the backend, plan for synchronisation: APIs that accept batched, delayed uploads, conflict handling and idempotent writes, plus API versioning, because installed app versions update slowly.

q: A team says 'we built a PWA, so it works offline'. What would you check?
a: That offline behaviour was designed: which screens and data are cached, how local writes are stored, and how they sync and resolve conflicts when the connection returns. A PWA can cache and work offline where the browser supports it, but the label doesn't make every feature offline-capable.

q: A web app needs to run a compute-heavy image filter in the browser, and the JavaScript version is too slow. What option does the lecture suggest, and what limits it?
a: WebAssembly: a portable instruction format run by a sandboxed runtime, well suited to compute-heavy modules in browsers or at the edge. It is limited by its host, which decides what capabilities it can access, so it speeds up computation but doesn't give the hardware access a native app has.

q: In a design review, someone lists 'use a replicated NoSQL store' under the system's characteristics. What is wrong with that, and how would you rewrite it?
a: That is a decision, not a characteristic. Characteristics are qualities to achieve, such as availability above 99.9% or tolerance of a zone failure. Decisions are the long-term choices made to achieve them, such as the replicated store. Write the characteristic first, then record the decision with the characteristic it serves, so it can be revisited if the requirement changes.

q: An architect delivered a full design document 6 months ago, and the developers have since quietly worked around half of it. What went wrong, and what model would fix it?
a: Hand-off architecture: the design was thrown over the wall and went stale as implementation realities appeared. Move to continuous collaboration, where the architect leads and mentors within the team and feedback from code changes the architecture. The cost is the architect's ongoing time, but the design stays true to the code.

q: A team must design a new system using Attribute Driven Design but starts by choosing a microservices pattern. What step have they skipped, and what should ADD produce?
a: They skipped the drivers: purpose, primary functionality, quality attributes, constraints and concerns. In ADD, design concepts such as patterns, tactics and reference architectures are chosen to satisfy those drivers. The outputs are structures: module views, component-and-connector views and allocation views (deployment, work assignment).

q: A startup with 4 developers is building an MVP whose features will change weekly. Monolith or microservices?
a: A modular monolith: one thing to build, deploy and debug, no network hops, and the team can't absorb microservices' operational overhead. Keep the modules well separated so a part that later needs independent scaling can be extracted. Revisit when the team or load grows.

q: After moving to microservices, a crash in the recommendation service still makes the whole product page time out. Why didn't fault isolation help, and what would?
a: Separate processes contain the crash, but the product page calls the recommendation service synchronously and waits, so the failure spreads through the call. Add timeouts, a circuit breaker and graceful degradation, such as showing the page without recommendations. Isolation is a property you have to design for; it doesn't come from deployment alone.

q: A team splitting a monolith asks what it gives up by moving to microservices. Give the two biggest costs for an e-commerce shop where Cart calls Catalog.
a: Distributed-system problems: Cart's call to Catalog now adds network latency and can fail partially. Data consistency also becomes harder across separate stores, for example keeping prices in carts aligned with the catalogue. Operational overhead grows as well: more deployments, monitoring and tracing. These costs are justified when independent scaling, releases and fault isolation are needed.

q: A team's order logic can only be tested against a real database and a running message broker, so tests take 20 minutes. How would hexagonal architecture change this?
a: Put the order logic in a domain core that depends only on ports (interfaces), with adapters for the database and broker on the outside. Tests then drive the domain through a test adapter and replace the database and broker with fakes, so business logic is tested in seconds. Keep a smaller set of integration tests for the real adapters.

q: A payments API has steady traffic around the clock and a strict 50 ms latency target. A teammate proposes serverless functions. Do you agree?
a: No. Cold starts threaten the latency target, and with constant usage the pay-per-use saving disappears. You also accept less control and lock-in. Long-running containers or VMs suit steady, latency-critical load. Serverless would fit sporadic, event-driven parts, such as sending receipts.

q: A team builds a function-based service and later wants to move part of it off that provider. How could combining hexagonal design with serverless have helped?
a: If the function's business logic sat in a hexagonal core, with the trigger and data stores as adapters, only the adapters would need rewriting to move providers or to run in a container. Serverless outsources infrastructure; hexagonal shields the domain from it. Together they reduce the lock-in cost of serverless.

q: A ride-hailing company needs surge prices updated within seconds and also retrains its pricing model on 3 years of trip history every night. Lambda or Kappa?
a: Lambda: a speed layer streams trip events for near-real-time surge prices, a batch layer recomputes the model over full history, and a serving layer exposes both. The cost is maintaining two pipelines that must agree. Kappa would be simpler if retraining could be done by replaying the stream, but reprocessing years of history through one stream engine is harder.

q: A monolith needs to notify inventory, email and analytics when an order is placed, and each new consumer currently means editing the order code. Must the team move to microservices to fix this?
a: No. Event-driven is a principle that can be applied on top of any style. The monolith can publish an 'order placed' event that consumers subscribe to, which gives loose coupling, lets consumers scale independently and adds new consumers without editing order code. The cost is eventual consistency and the need to monitor event flows.

q: A company runs one Kubernetes cluster in one region and must now serve EU customers whose data must stay in the EU. Which archetype helps, and what does it cost?
a: Multi-cluster or hybrid deployment: an EU cluster keeps EU workloads and data in the EU, puts compute closer to those users and limits the impact of one cluster failing. The cost is operating several clusters consistently, routing users to the right cluster, and the reporting and data work across them.

q: After adding app servers, the database becomes the bottleneck. Which scale-cube axis would you use next?
a: First identify the data-tier limit. If it's reads, replicas or caching help (x axis on the data tier). If it's writes on independent records, shard by a suitable key (z axis). Splitting off a heavy workload into its own service and store (y axis) isolates it. None of these fixes a poorly designed slow query, so check that first.

q: A team describes its 3-tier app (web, logic, database) as 'already microservices because it has separate tiers'. What is the structural difference?
a: 3-tier splits by technical layer, so one business change still touches every tier and they deploy together. Microservices split vertically by business capability, and each service owns its logic and data and deploys independently. The 3-tier app can scale tiers separately but not capabilities.

q: A SaaS's checkout path is overloaded during sales, but the search and account features are not. Which scale-cube axis fits, and why not just add more clones?
a: The y axis (functional decomposition): split checkout into its own service so it can scale on its own. Cloning the whole app (x axis) also scales search and accounts that don't need it, which wastes capacity, and it doesn't isolate checkout failures. The cost is a new service boundary and its data ownership.

q: A bad deploy to a multi-tenant SaaS took down all 4,000 customers at once. Which archetype limits this, and what does it cost?
a: Cell-based architecture: a router assigns tenants to independent full-stack cells with no cross-cell calls, and releases roll out cell by cell, so a bad deploy hits one cell first. With 10 equal cells, roughly 400 customers would be affected. Costs: duplicated capacity, a router that becomes critical, harder cross-cell reporting, and the automation to run many environments.

q: A team of five Java services proposes adding a sidecar service mesh for retries and telemetry. Would you approve it?
a: Probably not yet. A mesh adds an extra network hop, memory per pod and a control plane, and the lecture suggests it is rarely justified below about a dozen services in one language, where a shared library can give the same retries and telemetry. A requirement for uniform mTLS, or a move to several languages, would change the answer.

q: One front-end team builds a single web app and is considering micro-frontends to 'be modern'. What would you advise?
a: Don't. Micro-frontends extend team independence to the UI, which pays off when many teams share one UI or a legacy front end is being replaced piece by piece. With one team you take on duplicated payloads, design-consistency work and shared-state problems with no independence gained. A separate backend for each experience (BFF) may still help if web and mobile need different APIs.

q: A company bought a lakehouse and declared it has 'a data mesh'. What is missing?
a: A lakehouse is a storage and processing base (open table formats with ACID, schema evolution and time travel on object storage). Data mesh is an operating model: domain teams own their data as products with contracts and quality, on a self-serve platform under federated governance. Without domain ownership and governance maturity, it is still a central data platform.

q: A product team wants to run personalisation and A/B routing at the edge, and also move order checkout there for speed. Which part fits edge-native, and which doesn't?
a: Personalisation and A/B routing fit: they are light, latency-sensitive and can tolerate eventually consistent edge storage. Checkout needs strong consistency with the origin system of record, so keep it at the origin. Edge also brings limited runtimes, harder debugging and lock-in, so keep edge logic small.

q: A concert-ticketing app wants to be local-first so fans can pick seats offline. Where does local-first work here and where doesn't it?
a: It works for drafts, such as building a seat selection or a wishlist on the local replica. It can't guarantee that a seat is sold only once, because an offline replica doesn't know about other replicas' bookings, and CRDT-style merging doesn't protect global invariants. Confirm the purchase through an authoritative coordination step before promising the seat.

q: A retailer composes its commerce stack from a vendor cart, a vendor tax engine, in-house pricing and a headless CMS (MACH). Two years in, nobody knows who owns checkout failures. What went wrong?
a: Integration became the architecture without a capability map that names owners, so MACH turned into distributed procurement. Each packaged business capability needs a clear owner and integration contracts. Integration, identity and cost across many vendors are routinely underestimated.

q: A 12-developer company plans to build an internal developer platform with golden paths and self-service templates. Is it worth it?
a: Probably not yet. Platform engineering pays off when cognitive load limits delivery across many teams, and it must be run as a product, measured by adoption and DORA metrics. For 12 developers, shared templates and a simple pipeline may be enough. The risk at any size is the platform team becoming a gatekeeper instead of an enabler.

q: A bank wants to modernise a 15-year-old monolithic loan system used by 300 branches while continuing to issue loans every day. Propose a target style and a migration approach, and name the two biggest trade-offs.
a: Target microservices split by business capability (application, credit check, disbursement, notification), each owning its data, with hexagonal design inside services for testability and events between them for loose coupling. Migrate incrementally with a strangler approach, routing one capability at a time to new services, rather than a big-bang rewrite that would stop loan issuance. The trade-offs are distributed-system problems (latency, partial failures, consistency across stores) and operational overhead, so invest in observability and platform automation before the number of services grows.

q: Design a data architecture for a ride-hailing company that needs surge pricing within 5 seconds of demand changes and nightly retraining on 3 years of trips. Justify Lambda or Kappa, and say what would change your choice.
a: Lambda: a speed layer processes the trip-event stream for near-real-time surge prices, a batch layer holds full history and retrains models nightly, and a serving layer merges the results. Batch remains the accurate source of truth. The cost is two pipelines with logic that must stay consistent. Choose Kappa instead if reprocessing can be done by replaying the stream within the nightly window, which trades the second pipeline for harder stateful stream processing. Event-driven ingestion keeps producers decoupled either way.

q: A government services app must reach all citizens, including those on old phones. It needs form-filling that survives a dropped connection, and a later phase adds reading ID cards over NFC at kiosks. Native or PWA? Give the design implications for the backend services.
a: Start with a PWA: broad reach, no install barrier, one codebase and instant updates suit a citizen service. Design offline form drafts with local storage and sync. For the NFC kiosks, use a native or cross-platform native kiosk app, because hardware access through browsers varies, and the kiosks are controlled devices. Backend implications: APIs must accept delayed, batched submissions idempotently and handle conflicts, a separate backend for each experience (BFF) may serve web and kiosk clients, and API versioning is needed for installed kiosk apps.

q: An e-commerce site handles normal traffic but fails on Black Friday at 12 times the load: the database's write capacity is exhausted and checkout slows everything else. Apply the AKF scale cube to the problem and name a side effect of each change.
a: x axis: add load-balanced clones of the stateless web tier, plus read replicas; side effect: replica lag gives stale reads. y axis: split checkout into its own service and store so it scales and fails independently; side effect: cross-service consistency for orders and inventory. z axis: shard orders by customer or region to spread writes, which is the fix for exhausted write capacity; side effect: cross-shard queries and reporting become harder. Add a queue in front of order processing to level the peak.

q: A global SaaS needs sub-100 ms response for login and personalisation worldwide, must keep EU data in the EU, and had an outage last year where one bad deploy hit every tenant. Which modern archetypes would you combine, and what are their costs?
a: Cells per region and tenant group bound the blast radius and keep EU tenants' data in EU cells, with releases rolled out cell by cell. Edge-native functions handle authentication checks and personalisation near users, with the origin remaining the system of record. A platform with GitOps operates N cells consistently. The costs are duplicated infrastructure, a critical cell router, hard cross-cell reporting, eventual consistency and limited runtimes at the edge, and the investment in platform automation.

q: A new product will have 3 developers at launch, sporadic traffic from 0 to 2,000 requests a minute, and a plan to grow to 6 teams in 2 years. Compare monolith, microservices and serverless, and recommend a path.
a: A modular monolith minimises deployment and network complexity for 3 developers but scales as one unit. Microservices give independent scaling and releases but bring partial failures, data coordination and operational overhead the team can't afford yet. Serverless suits the sporadic load and costs little when idle, but brings cold starts, runtime limits and lock-in. Recommend a modular monolith, or a few functions with a hexagonal core for the spiky parts, with clear module boundaries so services can be extracted as the 6 teams arrive.

q: A team split its monolith into 6 separately deployed apps, but they still share one relational database, and every release still needs a joint change window. Why?
a: Shared tables mean a schema change for one app can break the others, so releases must be coordinated, and independent deployment is lost. Give each service private ownership of its data, with others reaching it through the service's API or events. The cost is that cross-service queries and consistency now need design.

q: In a monolith, ticket creation needs 10 times more capacity at peak, and the reporting module needs a newer library version that conflicts with the rest. Which monolith shortcomings are these, and how would microservices address them?
a: All-or-nothing scaling (the whole app must be cloned to scale one hot function) and library or technology lock-in (one dependency set for everything). As separate services, ticketing scales on its own and reporting picks its own stack. The price is network calls, separate deployments and more to monitor.

q: A new microservice keeps its config in a file inside the image and holds user sessions in memory. Which service principles does it break, and why do they matter for independence?
a: External configuration and stateless instances. Baked-in config means rebuilding to change environments. In-memory sessions mean instances can't be added or replaced freely. Move config outside the image and sessions to a shared store, while the service still owns its durable domain data in its own store.

q: A startup with 3 developers and a simple CRUD app asks whether to start with microservices. What is your advice?
a: Start with a monolith. For low-complexity systems the microservice premium (operations, monitoring, versioning, network calls) lowers productivity. Keep the code modular and split later when complexity, team size or scaling needs justify it.

q: The most-called function in a monolith is 'get customer', which nearly every module uses. A teammate wants to extract it first because it is the busiest. Do you agree?
a: Not on usage alone. A function that every module calls is tightly coupled, so extracting it first turns in-process calls into many chatty network calls and adds latency everywhere. Extract first a coherent business capability with a measurable scaling or change problem and dependencies you can separate. Heavy use is one signal, not the deciding one.

q: A company adopts microservices but keeps separate UI, DBA, test and server teams, and every feature now needs four teams. What is missing?
a: The organisational shift. Microservices assume small cross-functional teams that own a service end to end. With layer-based teams, every change crosses team boundaries and independence is lost. Reorganise around services, or the system takes on microservice overhead without the delivery benefit.

q: Using the four AKF pressures, should a company split out its payment capability, which changes rarely but must stay available during catalogue outages?
a: Probably yes, driven by availability and fault tolerance: payment is business-critical and should not fail when the catalogue does. Developer throughput gives little reason, since it changes rarely. Weigh this against cost, because a separate service adds operations, and against the scalability of its data and dependencies.

q: Only ticket creation is busy during a concert sale; search and catalogue are quiet. Compare how a monolith and microservices scale, and what each costs.
a: The monolith clones the whole application behind a load balancer, paying for idle search and catalogue copies. Microservices scale only Ticketing, for example to 3 instances, while Search and Catalog stay at 1. The microservices approach costs separate deployments, discovery and monitoring, which pays off when load differs this much.

q: A product team wants to try a hotel-recommendation feature in the booking flow and drop it if it fails. Why is this easier with microservices, and what still needs care?
a: Experimentation and substitution: a new, self-contained service plugs into the existing flow and can be removed without touching the rest, so the team can fail fast. Care is still needed with the API contract, timeouts and fallbacks, so the booking flow keeps working if the experiment is slow or removed.

q: An analytics team wants to subscribe to the existing order-events topic for a new dashboard, and says 'no impact analysis is needed because the publisher doesn't change'. Do you agree?
a: Partly. The publisher's code doesn't change, which is the benefit of event-driven design. But the new consumer must understand the event contract, retention and authorisation, and handle duplicates, and a future change to the event schema now has one more consumer to consider. Register the consumer and its contract assumptions.

q: A pricing service needs a breaking change, but 3 partner integrations can't upgrade for 6 months. How can microservices handle this?
a: Each service packages its own runtime, so V1 and V2 can run side by side. A gateway rule routes the partners to V1 and other clients, or one region, to V2. Retire V1 once the partners migrate. The cost is running and supporting two versions, including any data both must read.

q: Decompose a food-delivery app (place order, assign rider, track delivery, pay, rate restaurant) using the three-step method. Where would you put 'assign rider'?
a: Step 1 lists the system operations above. Step 2 identifies services by business capability: Order, Dispatch, Tracking, Payment, Ratings. Step 3 assigns each operation and defines APIs. 'Assign rider' belongs to Dispatch, which owns rider availability, and it collaborates with Order through an event or API. Putting it in Order would make Order own rider data it shouldn't.

q: Two services need to update an order and an inventory record together, and a teammate proposes a distributed transaction across both databases. What does the lecture's decentralised-data characteristic suggest?
a: Avoid distributed transactions: each service owns its database, and the services coordinate through their APIs or events, with compensating actions if a step fails. This keeps services independently deployable. The cost is eventual consistency and designing for failed or repeated steps.

q: An architect says 'our SOA already has services, so we have microservices'. The SOA routes everything through a central enterprise bus and several services share a database. What is the difference?
a: Microservices emphasise independent deployment, lightweight communication and private data ownership. A central bus that holds integration logic, plus a shared database, couples services in deployment and data. SOA doesn't require a central bus, but this one has one. To move toward microservices, move logic out of the bus and give each service its own data.

q: A team has deployed 8 services, but ops can't tell which one failed in an incident, and each service has its own way of reading config. Which platform building blocks are missing?
a: Diagnosability and monitoring (central logs, metrics, tracing) and configuration management. A microservice chassis for cross-cutting concerns would standardise both. Service discovery and an API gateway are also needed for finding services and outside access. These capabilities are what make many small services operable.

q: An exam answer lists a dozen product names for a microservices platform. What should replace the list to score well?
a: The capability each tool provides and why the design needs it: an API gateway for external access, a service registry or platform DNS for discovery, monitoring and tracing for diagnosability, a CI/CD pipeline and registry for delivery. Name a product only as an example of a category. The marks are for matching capabilities to requirements, not for recalling products.

q: A team releases a risky change to a payment service. Should they use a canary release or blue-green, and what does each give up?
a: A canary sends a small slice of traffic to the new version first, which limits exposure and gives real-traffic evidence, but both versions run at once, so they must be compatible. Blue-green switches all traffic between two environments in one step, which gives a fast, clean rollback but needs double capacity and exposes everyone at once. For a risky payment change, a canary is usually safer.

q: A team on Kubernetes plans to install a separate service registry. What would you ask before approving it?
a: Whether the platform already provides discovery: Kubernetes DNS and Services already resolve and load-balance service names. A separate registry adds another component that must stay highly available. It is justified when services span environments outside the cluster or need registry features the platform lacks.

q: When an order is placed, the Order service calls Payment, Inventory and Notification synchronously, and an outage in Notification makes orders fail. Redesign the communication.
a: Keep a synchronous, time-bounded call only where the order needs an immediate result, such as payment authorisation. Publish an 'order placed' event to a durable topic for notification and other deferred work, so a Notification outage delays emails instead of failing orders. The cost is eventual consistency and handling retries, ordering and duplicate events.

q: Internal services exchange large volumes of small messages, and JSON parsing is a measurable cost. A public partner API also exists. Would you use gRPC, REST/JSON or both?
a: Both. gRPC fits the internal calls: schema-defined binary messages over HTTP/2 are compact and fast to parse across languages, and they support streaming. REST/JSON fits the partner API: self-describing and widely supported by web clients and tooling. Check proxy and browser support before using gRPC beyond internal traffic.

q: An API uses POST /api for every action, with the action name in the request body, and the team wonders why responses can't be cached. Which REST maturity level is this, and what would you change?
a: Level 0: one URL with everything POSTed. Move to resources (Level 1) and proper HTTP verbs (Level 2), so reads become GET requests that web infrastructure can cache, and writes use POST, PUT or DELETE. Level 3 would add links to next actions (HATEOAS), which helps discoverability but is optional for most internal APIs.

q: A team switched to reactive, non-blocking code and says 'our services are now decoupled from their dependencies'. Is that right?
a: No. Reactive code changes how a process waits, so threads aren't blocked, but the service still depends on its downstream calls succeeding and has no delivery guarantee. Decoupling comes from asynchronous messaging through a durable queue or topic, together with timeouts and fallbacks.

q: A mobile app's home screen makes 9 calls to different services and is slow on poor networks. What would you change?
a: Add an API gateway (or a backend for the mobile client) that calls the services and composes one response tailored to the screen, cutting round trips and payload size for limited mobile bandwidth. The gateway becomes a critical component that must be highly available and must not accumulate business logic.

q: A polyglot estate (Java, Go, Python) uses client-side discovery with a registry library, and the Python library is unmaintained. What are the options?
a: Switch to server-side discovery: clients call a load balancer or platform service name that queries the registry, so no discovery code is needed per language. The cost is another component that must be highly available, unless the platform, such as Kubernetes, already provides it. Client-side discovery saves a hop but needs library support in every language.

q: A team adds an optional request field and a new response attribute and calls it version 2.0.0. Is MAJOR right?
a: Usually not: this is MINOR if omitting the field keeps the old meaning and existing consumers ignore unknown response fields. A MAJOR bump wrongly signals a breaking change and can trigger unnecessary migrations. Test those consumer assumptions, because a new required field or a changed meaning would be MAJOR.

q: A downstream inventory service is often unavailable for minutes at a time, and the order service's threads pile up waiting. Give the cause, a countermeasure and the countermeasure's drawback.
a: The cause is synchronous calls with no timeout, so failures propagate as blocked threads. Set client timeouts with clear errors, and where delayed processing is acceptable send work through a durable queue with acknowledgements and bounded retries, with idempotent handlers. The drawback is that orders are confirmed before stock is checked, so the business needs a path for orders that later fail.

q: A company with waterfall releases, physical servers and monitoring of infrastructure only wants to move to 50 microservices this year. What does the maturity model suggest?
a: It is at a low level on the process, infrastructure and monitoring dimensions, which is a warning sign. With 50 services, missing DevOps, containers and APM with central logs would make troubleshooting and releases unmanageable. Raise maturity first: automate delivery, containerise, centralise logs and tracing, then grow the service count.

q: A discount rule applies only within the cart service, while a loyalty rule spans cart, orders and partners. Where should each rule live?
a: The simple, local discount rule fits an embedded rule engine inside the cart service. The cross-domain loyalty rule belongs in a central rule repository that the services consult, so it is defined once. An end-to-end process that also involves people would be composed with BPM or a dashboard.

q: A retailer's monolithic e-commerce app slows down at sale peaks (search traffic rises 10 times, checkout 3 times), and releases take 6 weeks because 5 teams share one deployable. Propose a microservices design and an incremental migration plan, and name the main risk at each stage.
a: Decompose by business capability: Catalog/Search, Cart, Order, Inventory, Payment. Assign operations and define APIs, giving each service its own data, behind an API gateway with service discovery. Extract Search first: it has the biggest load difference, it is read-heavy and its data can be copied. Then extract Cart and Order. Risks: at first, data synchronisation between the new Search store and the monolith; later, consistency between Order, Inventory and Payment without distributed transactions. Independent deployment through CI/CD addresses the 6-week release cycle, but only if teams are reorganised around services.

q: A 6-person team with manual deployments, infrastructure-only monitoring and a moderately complex internal app is told to 'go microservices'. Argue whether they should, using the microservice premium and the maturity model, and say what would change your answer.
a: They shouldn't yet. The microservice premium (operations, monitoring, versioning, network latency, troubleshooting) pays off only when a system is too complex to manage as a monolith, and a moderately complex app for 6 people is unlikely to qualify. Low maturity on process and monitoring makes it worse, because they couldn't diagnose distributed failures. Build a modular monolith and raise DevOps maturity. Reconsider if the team grows, parts need very different scaling or availability, or release coordination becomes the bottleneck.

q: Design the communication between Order, Payment, Inventory and Notification services for a shop that must confirm payment to the user within 3 seconds and must never charge twice. Justify each synchronous or asynchronous choice.
a: Order calls Payment synchronously with a time limit under the 3-second budget, because the user needs the outcome, and passes an idempotency key so a retry never charges twice. After payment, Order publishes an 'order paid' event to a durable topic: Inventory reserves stock and Notification sends email asynchronously, so their outages don't fail checkout. Persist order and payment state and handle duplicate events in consumers. If inventory later fails, compensate by refunding or back-ordering instead of using a distributed transaction. gRPC can carry the internal calls.

q: A system has 40 services, a mobile app and a web app. Explain the roles of an API gateway, a service registry and a service mesh, say which traffic each handles, and say which you could do without if the platform is Kubernetes.
a: The gateway handles north-south traffic from the mobile and web apps: routing, composition, security, throttling, protocol translation and monitoring. It can be tailored per client type. The registry records where service instances live, for client-side or server-side discovery. The mesh manages east-west traffic between the 40 services: retries, encryption and telemetry. On Kubernetes, the platform's Services and DNS already provide discovery, so a separate registry is often unnecessary. The mesh is justified at 40 services if uniform policy is needed, at the cost of extra hops and a control plane.

q: A public pricing API is used by 200 external clients. The team must rename a field, add an optional discount field and fix a rounding bug. Plan the version numbers and the rollout so no client breaks.
a: Rounding fix: PATCH. Optional discount field: MINOR, provided omitting it keeps the old meaning and clients ignore unknown response fields, which should be tested with consumer contracts. Renaming a field is incompatible: MAJOR. Run V1 and V2 side by side, route by version at the gateway, document both contracts with OpenAPI, and retire V1 only after the 200 clients have migrated, tracked through gateway metrics. The cost is supporting two versions for the migration period.

q: A team designs a highly available Kubernetes control plane as 'one active master and one standby master'. What does this description hide?
a: Each control-plane component has its own availability model. API servers can serve concurrently behind a load balancer, controllers and schedulers use leader election so only one acts at a time, and etcd needs a quorum, usually an odd number of members. A single active/standby pair can lose etcd quorum or leave API requests unserved, so design each component's replication and recovery separately.

q: A traditional web app keeps user sessions in each app server's memory and uses cookies to hold session IDs. A teammate says going cloud native means disabling cookies. Do you agree?
a: No. A cookie can still carry a session identifier or token. The scaling problem is session state that lives only on one replaceable instance. Move sessions to a shared store, or use suitable client-held tokens, so any replica can serve the next request. The cookie transport and where the state lives are separate choices.

q: In the delivery toolchain (language, data store, build, deploy, release tracking), a team picks a vector database as its main store 'because it's modern'. The app records orders and payments. What is wrong?
a: Each link in the toolchain should be justified by requirements. Orders and payments need transactions and integrity, which point to relational or NewSQL stores. A vector store serves similarity search, for example for RAG, and could sit alongside them. Modern options are added where they help, not as automatic replacements.

q: A company wants to replace its SOAP web services and ESB-based workflows. What cloud-native options does the instructor map them to, and what caution applies?
a: SOAP services can become Kubernetes services exposed through API gateways with REST. ESB and BPEL orchestration can move toward events and lightweight orchestration, and in the instructor's list toward agent harnesses with evals and human validation. Replace selected integrations where requirements justify it, since none of these automatically replaces every working mechanism, and agent workflows need verification.

q: A 6-person team wants independent deployment for three areas of its product but can't operate dozens of services. Microservices, monolith or something between?
a: A microlith, the instructor's term for a coarse-grained deployable between a monolith and microservices: three independently deployable units, each with some independent scaling, and far fewer moving parts than fine-grained services. It suits teams without the operational maturity for many services. Split further later if one area needs it.

q: A team says 'we moved from VMs to containers to functions, so we are now properly decomposed by business function'. Is that right?
a: No. Packaging and decomposition are separate decisions. A VM can host several services, a container can hold a monolith, and a function can be one handler inside a service. Decompose by business capability and operating needs first, then choose the execution unit for each part. Replication and data partitioning are further, independent scaling decisions.

q: Decompose a streaming app's search, profile, playback-resume and title-row recommendations into services, choosing a data store for each with a reason.
a: Search: a search index or document store for text queries. Profile: relational or key-value, for structured per-user data. Playback resume position: a fast key-value store, written often and read by user and title. Recommendations: a service fed by viewing events, which precomputes the title rows into a fast read store. Each store adds operational cost, so share stores where the access patterns match.

q: Decompose a Netflix-like streaming platform into a cloud-native architecture: identify services and data stores, how viewing events reach recommendations, how it is deployed, and how it scales on each axis.
a: Services: search, profile, catalogue, recommendations and playback, each with a fitting store (search index, relational or key-value, document, precomputed fast reads, and key-value for resume position). Viewing events flow through a stream into recommendation processing, Kappa-style. Run stateless services as Kubernetes Deployments behind Services and an API gateway, using tokens or shared session state so any replica can serve. Scale by replication (more replicas), functional decomposition (hot services such as playback scale alone) and partitioning (shard user data by user ID). The costs are eventual consistency in recommendations and more services to operate.

q: Modernise a traditional web app that uses server-side sessions in memory, SOAP services, an ESB for workflows and a relational database. Decide what to keep, what to change and why.
a: Keep the relational database for transactional data and keep cookies, but move sessions to a shared store or tokens so replicas are replaceable. Expose SOAP functions through an API gateway with REST, rewriting services only where change justifies it. Move ESB workflows toward events or lightweight orchestration one flow at a time. Add observability and automated delivery (CI/CD or GitOps) first, because they make every later change safer. Don't swap in a vector store or agents unless a requirement calls for them.

q: Explain how Kubernetes provides high availability for both the control plane and the applications, and say why a large replica count alone doesn't guarantee availability to users.
a: Control plane: replicate API servers behind a load balancer, run controllers and schedulers with leader election, and keep etcd with quorum across failure domains. Applications: run ready replicas spread across zones, with health probes so kubelet restarts failed containers and controllers replace lost Pods, and persistent data with its own replication and recovery. Replica count alone doesn't help if replicas share one zone, lack capacity headroom, depend on a single database, or fail readiness together, so availability must be designed end to end.

q: A new product will start with one team and modest load but expects to grow. Choose between a singular and a distributed architecture, and explain how you would leave room to evolve.
a: Choose a singular, modular architecture: simplicity and low latency outweigh independent scaling at this size. Keep clear internal boundaries by business capability, make it stateless and containerised so replication works from day one, and keep data ownership per module so the parts can later be split into microliths or microservices. Real systems end up hybrid, so plan the first split around the module most likely to need independent scaling.

q: A manager says 'we went serverless, so we no longer need to think about failures or state'. Correct this.
a: Serverless means the provider operates the servers, OS and scaling, not that servers or failures vanish. The team still designs durable state in external stores, retries, timeouts and protection for downstream dependencies, and configures each function's access and limits. Built-in availability covers the platform, not the application's own logic or the services it calls.

q: A team plans to turn its 8 microservices into 120 single-action functions 'because FaaS is the next maturity stage'. Do you agree?
a: No. Decomposition (one app, domain services, individual actions) and hosting (servers, containers, functions) are separate choices, and moving to FaaS is not a required next stage. A microservice can be implemented with one or a few functions behind its API. 120 functions add deployment, monitoring and coordination overhead. Split further only where an action has different scaling, timing or ownership needs.

q: A function processes a stream of account events and must apply each account's events in order. What should the team check, and what doesn't the platform guarantee?
a: Check the stream's ordering scope: streams usually keep order within a partition or shard, so events must be partitioned by account ID. Check retry behaviour too, because a failing batch can block or reorder processing. The platform doesn't automatically protect downstream dependencies, so configure retries, timeouts and failure handling as needed.

q: A single function validates an order, charges the card, updates stock and sends an email. What principle does this break, and what would you change?
a: Single-purpose functions: one function doing four things is harder to test, fails as a unit, and its side effects (a charge without an email) are hard to reason about. Split it into a push-based pipeline in which each step triggers the next through events. The cost is coordinating the steps and handling a failure part-way through.

q: A video platform transcodes uploads that arrive in bursts of hundreds after events, with nothing in between. Is serverless a good fit, and why?
a: Yes. Data processing and transcoding is a typical use case: work is triggered by events, can run in parallel on stateless compute, and you pay only during bursts. Check the platform's execution time and memory limits against the longest video. Very long transcodes may need a container or batch service instead.

q: An order workflow can take hours while waiting for warehouse confirmation. Must one function stay running throughout?
a: No. Persist workflow state in a durable store and use events or scheduled steps to invoke short functions as each piece of work becomes ready. A long-running service is justified only if the work truly needs continuous execution or the orchestration overhead outweighs its benefit.

q: A latency-critical API runs at a steady 3,000 requests a second all day. A teammate argues serverless will be cheaper and faster. Evaluate this.
a: Doubtful on both counts. With steady high load, the pay-per-invocation advantage shrinks, so compare sustained-use cost against always-on containers.
